19903-the-american-missionary-volume-49-:
The American Missionary for May 1895 is volume 49, number 5. Its front matter lists auditors like Peter McCarter of Bible House, New York. The executive committee includes William Hayes Ward and Charles L. Lyman. District secretaries cover Congregational House in Boston and La Salle Street, Chicago. The American Missionary Association ran this monthly for its supporters. Names and offices fill these administrative pages.

Such lists map a national benevolent machine. The Association's schools served freedpeople across the South. Its magazine reported fields from Dakota to China. May 1895 catches the organization mid-stream, fully staffed. Researchers trace personnel through pages like these. The issue is a brick in a large archive.
22810-midnight-in-beauchamp-row-1895:
A bag stuffed with bank notes sits at the center of Midnight in Beauchamp Row, a short mystery tale dated 1895. Ned brings the money home, and his wife begs him not to leave her alone with it for the night. Their maid Tennie has gone off for a holiday, so the house stands empty except for the couple and the cash.

Fear does most of the work in the telling. Every sound in the dark house raises the stakes, and the wife's dread turns an ordinary evening into a vigil. Readers get a compact crime story built on suspense rather than gore, the kind of tale that filled magazines of the period. It rewards anyone who likes a tight plot, a house at night, and money that invites trouble.
aksakov-animisme-et-spiritisme-1895:
Alexander Aksakov sorts strange feats in two great heaps in Animisme et spiritisme, in French from 1895. Aksakov was a man of state in Russia and a chief of the field in Europe. Some feats, he says, come from the seer's own hid self: that heap is animism. The rest need the dead at work: that heap is spiritism, his true faith.

Tests and famed cases fill two fat tomes in proof. His split gave the field words it still uses each day. The book, in French, is its great sort. Few works shaped its terms so much.
arxiv-2511-20195:
Itaba and Minaki complete a dimension formula for a family of noncommutative algebras. Their 2025 paper computes Hochschild cohomology of Beilinson algebras. The algebras come from graded down-up algebras with weights. Those down-up algebras are cubic AS-regular of dimension three. Weights are coprime integers n and m here.

Earlier work covered the cases where n equals one. Belmans handled the smallest case, both weights one. Itaba and Ueyama covered n one with larger m. The new formula handles all weights at least two. Dimensions of each cohomology group are given explicitly. A striking byproduct follows for m bigger than n. The derived category of the associated noncommutative scheme differs fundamentally. It matches no smooth projective surface's derived category. The ring structure is also determined fully. Yoneda products on cohomology are described for all weights. Noncommutative geometry gains complete invariants for this family.
arxiv-2511-20395:
Schoppema and colleagues hunt environmental clues behind a shellfish poison. Their 2025 paper studies tetrodotoxin in bivalve mollusks. The toxin, famous from pufferfish, appeared in European waters in 2012. Contaminated shellfish threaten food safety and cause economic losses. Early prediction would help the industry and regulators. Prior work blamed shallow habitats and warm water.

The team built an explainable deep learning model for prediction. Its setting was the Dutch Zeeland estuary. Inputs were weather and water measurements over time. The output was simply whether contamination was present. Sunrise time, sunset time, and global radiation mattered most. Water temperature and chloride concentration also contributed strongly. Day length and total sun hours thus drive contamination risk. The explainable outputs make the model trustworthy for authorities. It offers a practical tool against marine toxin risks.
arxiv-2511-20495:
Bodart, Ron-George, and Yadin finish a sorting of groups by their geometric edge. Their 2025 note studies Cayley graphs of groups built from finite generator sets. Busemann functions measure distance relative to a fixed basepoint. Closing their set adds points at infinity, forming an edge. How many such points a group has reflects its large-scale shape.

The theorem: finitely many Busemann points forces the group to be virtually cyclic. Such groups are nearly just the integers in disguise. Combined with earlier work, this completes the full sorting. Every group with a finite such edge is now classified. A new notion called annihilators drives the proof. The edge stays fixed under the group's own action. Metric-functionals were proposed as analogues of linear functionals for spaces. Support came from the Israel Science Foundation. Finite edges turn out to be extremely restrictive.
arxiv-2511-20595:
Laguë and colleagues read galaxy feedback's fingerprint in the microwave sky's motion signal. Their 2025 paper builds the first fully data-driven emulator of matter clustering. Star formation and black holes blow gas around, reshaping small-scale structure. That baryonic feedback muddies cosmological inferences from lensing. Fitting formulas exist, but their knobs are not observable.

The kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect traces free electrons around halos. Its power spectrum shape correlates with feedback's suppression pattern. A neural network learns that mapping from simulations. Training used the FLAMINGO suite spanning many feedback recipes. The emulator rebuilds the matter power spectrum to sub-percent accuracy. That holds for scales up to five and redshifts 0.2 to 1.25 in their tests. Unseen feedback models and cosmologies stay near percent-level too. A forecast pairs Simons Observatory maps with DESI galaxies. Feedback and new physics can finally be told apart.
arxiv-2511-20795:
Souradeep Dutta and colleagues report in 2025 a small rebuild of KRISP, a Facebook AI model that answers questions about images by consulting a structured knowledge graph. The original was built for industrial-scale training and is heavy and bound to a large backbone. The team's lightweight reproduction keeps the concept, neural embeddings grounded by explicit knowledge, slashing parameters for edge devices like phones and AR-VR headsets.

Their model freezes CLIP encoders for vision and text, projects the 512-dimensional features, and queries a local ConceptNet graph using question keywords and recognised image concepts. On the DAQUAR dataset and a synthetic proof-of-concept set, the replica reached about 75 percent of the original's performance. The rebuild also exposed design flaws, hidden assumptions, and practical pitfalls the original paper never discussed, documented through ablations. Confined to the graph's domain, the model refuses to hallucinate outside it.
arxiv-2511-20895:
Kimia Ahmadi and Wouter A. Serdijn improve in 2025 the circuit logic that squeezes maximum power from small solar cells. Their target is a head-mounted optical power receiver for freely moving rodents in neuroscience experiments, where light levels swing fast. Classic perturb-and-observe tracking wobbles around the peak. Their algorithm adds adaptive gradient descent: the step size scales with the power-voltage slope, cutting tracking time and steady-state oscillation. An optional start-up routine hunts the global peak under partial shading.

Simulations and measured rodent-derived light data show tracking efficiency of 99.94 percent under standard test conditions and 99.21 percent on experimental data. Temperature profiles stayed above 99.6 percent, and the shading routine added up to 7.8 percent under partial shading. A gate-level complexity analysis and a combined figure of merit place the method ahead of 35 rival perturb-and-observe algorithms.
arxiv-2511-21295:
Wenbo Fan and Weihua Gu propose a new kind of shared transit in 2025, built from small electric vehicles that team up and split apart. Earlier modular bus ideas needed vehicles to couple while moving and passengers to transfer mid-ride, technology far from ready. Fly-by transit instead pairs cheap trailer modules, which run solo feeder trips to each rider's door, with high-performance leader modules that haul coupled trailers in fast platoons along trunk lines.

Fan and Gu couple trailers only while stationary at hubs, then release the tail trailer on the move so the convoy never stops for drop-offs. A stylized corridor model optimizes the design and compares it with buses and ride-hailing taxis. Fly-by transit cut travel times versus buses and operating costs versus taxis. Its economies of scale beat both rivals, saving more than 13 percent in generalized system costs.
arxiv-2511-21395:
Qixun Wang and seven coauthors teach a multimodal AI to think in pictures it never has to draw, in 2025. Models that reason with images usually fetch or generate real pictures mid-thought, chained to external tools. Their framework, Monet, instead lets the model reason inside its latent visual space, producing continuous internal embeddings that act as visual thoughts, a style of abstract picturing closer to human imagination.

Wang and his coauthors train Monet with a three-stage distillation pipeline on Monet-SFT-125K, a new dataset of 125,000 interleaved text-and-image reasoning traces covering real photos, charts, text reading, and geometry. They also introduce VLPO, a reinforcement learning rule that grades the latent visual thoughts directly, after finding the standard GRPO rule mostly sharpens text reasoning instead. The resulting Monet-7B improves across perception and reasoning benchmarks and generalizes strongly to abstract visual puzzles outside its training mix.
arxiv-2511-21495:
Saurabh Gupta, Dmitry Bykov, Tracy Northup, and Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero work out how to chill a levitated nanoparticle using ions as a refrigerator, in 2025. Both objects float in the same dual-frequency Paul trap, an electric cage, and they interact through their Coulomb repulsion. The ions can be laser-cooled directly, a trick called Doppler cooling, while the nanoparticle cannot, so the team asks whether the cold ions can sympathetically drain the particle's motion through their coupling.

Gupta and his coauthors derive the system's quantum master equation and compute the cooling in detail. A single continuously cooled ion should bring the nanoparticle below 1 kelvin, even with the trap's micromotion jitter and no feedback control. Adding ions helps in direct proportion: the cooling rate grows linearly with ion count. With the shared motion of 12 ions, the forecast drops to tenths of a millikelvin, deep into the quantum regime experimentalists want.
arxiv-2511-21595:
Mauro Bernardi, Antonio Canale, and Marco Stefanucci fill a measurement gap for adaptive regression methods, in a 2025 statistics paper. Effective degrees of freedom say how much information a fitted model really uses, guiding model choice and error estimates. The classic Lasso penalty has a neat formula, but its adaptive descendants, which set penalty weights from a first-pass fit, had no equivalent theory despite wide use.

Bernardi and his coauthors derive the first unbiased estimator of the Adaptive Lasso's effective degrees of freedom, and the Adaptive Group Lasso's. Within Stein's unbiased risk estimation framework, they cover designs with independent or correlated predictors. The formulas contain inflation terms driven by the penalty size, the signs of fitted coefficients, and the least-squares estimates themselves. Tests on synthetic and real data show the payoff: sharper model choice and unbiased error estimates, putting adaptive methods on their parent's footing.
arxiv-2511-21695:
Ruchira Dhar and thirteen coauthors argue that how AI models are scored deserves its own standard card, in 2025. Models now release rapidly and openly, yet test reports remain scattered and uneven. Surveying recent work, the team identifies three persistent failures. Results cannot be reproduced, reports defeat non-specialists, and write-ups are too weak for emerging governance rules.

Their proposal, Evaluation Disclosure Cards or EvalCards, puts testing at the center, where Model Cards and BenchmarkCards leave it peripheral. The format prizes brevity: cards should take little effort to write or to read, and resist gaming. Uniform cards would make test details visible and consistent across releases. Researchers gain firmer ground for cumulative work, adopters a basis for informed choices, and regulators the transparency governance frameworks demand. The paper treats the card itself as research infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-00695:
Manoj Belavadi and Kathie Cameron wrote a 2025 graph theory paper on Kempe changes. A graph coloring assigns colors to points so that linked points differ. Pick two colors, and the points using them split into connected groups called Kempe chains. A Kempe swap flips the two colors inside one chain.

Swaps turn one valid coloring into another, so they map out how colorings connect. Belavadi and Cameron study graphs that avoid a fixed pattern graph, known as H-free graphs. Knowing when swaps can move between all colorings helps solve counting and sampling problems. It also bears on puzzles and timetables, where colorings model the choices.
arxiv-2512-01195:
Tao Luo, Yu Ning, and Xiande Zhang study the quantum chromatic number of certain graphs in a 2025 math paper. The chromatic number of a graph is the fewest colors needed so adjacent vertices differ. In the quantum version, players use entangled states to color cooperatively, sometimes with fewer colors than any classical method allows.

Few graph families have known quantum chromatic numbers. Orthogonality graphs are a notable exception, fully determined already. The authors study subgraphs of those graphs, and the distance-two Hamming graph, where words differing in few positions connect. Pinning down exact values shows where quantum strategies truly help.
arxiv-2512-01295:
Mihai Christodorescu and co-authors set out the safety needs for AI agents. Agents are programs that plan and act on their own. They use tools, read files, and send messages. A safe model alone does not make a safe full system.

The authors look at the whole system, not just the model. They list short-term and long-term research tasks for agent safety and privacy. Each task asks how an agent can be tricked, leak data, or cause harm. Their plan gives builders a shared map for tests, guards, and design rules that cover real use.
arxiv-2512-01495:
Joanne Lin and co-authors tackle video segmentation in dark clips. The task marks each object in each frame. Low light brings noise, blur, and low contrast. Both humans and machines find it hard. Large labeled sets for dark video are scarce too.

Fake dark clips made by past pipelines miss how real dark video degrades over time. The team's method, ELVIS, aims to lift low-light clips for better segmentation. Clearer input helps the model track objects through dark frames. Gains would aid night driving, security, and wildlife film work. The method is tested on real dark footage, not just bright clips dimmed by hand, which makes its scores harder to game.
arxiv-2512-01795:
Torrecilla Pinero and co-authors quantify risk in Voronoi service area models. Voronoi maps assign each place to its nearest service point. Straight-line distance drives that assignment. Rules like waste proximity principles rest on such maps in law.

In rough terrain or sparse infrastructure, straight lines mislead. True travel can be far longer than the map suggests. The team measures the misallocation risk that follows. Safer maps would assign services by real routes, which matters for equity in rural regions. Road-network distance is the natural fix the study points to, since travel time, not raw meters, decides who can reach a service.
arxiv-2512-01895:
Moving a facial expression from one face to another is easy within photos of real people and much harder across styles, say from a photograph to a cartoon. Avirup Dey and Vinay Namboodiri present StyleYourSmile in 2025, a method for retargeting faces across such domains without paired training examples in each style.

The hard part is keeping identity, expression, and style separate, so one can change without dragging the others along. Earlier methods often failed to generalize across domains, or needed slow test-time tuning and carefully built multi-style datasets. A method that skips those demands would make stylized animation and avatar tools far easier to build.
arxiv-2512-02095:
The Milky Way's small satellite galaxies are fossils of galaxy formation, but reading them requires separating chance variation from the physics of gas and stars. Jonah Rose and a large collaboration analyze in 2025 over a thousand simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies from the DREAMS Project.

The simulations use the TNG galaxy-formation model inside a standard cosmology, varying both the physics of ordinary matter and the cosmological settings. With so many hosts, each with its own environment and history, the team can disentangle halo-to-halo variance from the effects of baryonic feedback. The satellite populations that result give observers a sharper baseline for judging the real Milky Way.
arxiv-2512-02295:
Some spots on the Sun spout jets time and time again, like geysers. Each blast frees magnetic force stored low in the Sun's air. Aabha Monga and four co-authors probe in 2025 what drives these jets. They home in on how flows of magnetic flux meet and clash.

Flux that rises and flux that cancels out are known to feed jet birth. But what reloads one spot for blast after blast is still not clear. The team tracks how flux fields clash and build stress anew. The work feeds the broad study of how the Sun's magnetism drives blasts that can reach Earth.
arxiv-2512-02495:
Ali Mohammad-Djafari, Ning Chu, and Li Wang tackle inverse problems, where hidden causes must be inferred from indirect, noisy data. Such problems turn up across science and engineering, from medical scans to earth sensing. They are often ill posed, meaning small noise can cause large swings in the answer.

Classic fixes include regularization, which adds prior rules, and Bayesian inference, which tracks uncertainty openly. The authors combine Bayesian thinking with physics informed neural networks, which respect known physical laws. Their test case is infrared image processing, where cleaner inference could sharpen heat based pictures used in inspection and diagnosis. In plain terms, the method lets the data speak but keeps wild guesses in check.
arxiv-2512-02695:
Md Faysal Hossain and Sean B. Andersson track single tiny particles in real time as they move inside cells. Feedback driven tracking measures light from a labeled particle and steers the instrument to follow it. Watching one particle in its native setting reveals motion that snapshots cannot show.

Their double helix based method shapes the light so position can be read quickly and well. Fast, accurate estimates feed the control loop that keeps the particle centered. Better tracking opens longer, clearer views of transport and binding inside living cells, key processes in health and disease. Long clean tracks beat short bright ones when the goal is to watch a cell at work over time.
arxiv-2512-02795:
Marcus Kessel argues that code generating AI should learn from watching software run, not just reading it. Today's models train on static artifacts: source code, comments, and specifications. They rarely see recorded behavior, so they can absorb buggy or mislabeled code as if it were truth.

Deep facts about a program cannot be decided in general, so observed runs are the practical ground truth. Kessel proposes observation lakehouses: living, interactive archives of software behavior. Feeding models real execution traces could teach them what code does, not just what it looks like, cutting confident errors. Runs leave a trail that reads can check, and that trail is the part most code tools throw out too soon.
arxiv-2512-03195:
Matching job ads to skill lists is slow work by hand. Stylianos Saroglou and co-authors test language models for that task in this 2025 work. They link job vacancy texts to two European frameworks for skills and qualifications.

One framework, ESCO, lists skills, competences, and occupations. The other, EQF, sets levels for qualifications. The authors compare two methods from past work, sentence linking and entity linking. Better linking could help job seekers find fitting roles. It could also help schools see which skills employers want most. Public job services could use such links to guide training funds toward real demand.
arxiv-2512-03395:
Ratios of partition functions can reveal phase transitions. Satoshi Morita and Naoki Kawashima compute such ratios with tensor renormalization in this 2025 work. At criticality, theory predicts universal values for these dimensionless ratios.

Those values come from conformal field theory through partition functions on a torus. Tensor methods let the authors compute the ratios in practice. Matching theory and computation is a strong check on both. The approach helps study critical phenomena in magnets and other many-body systems. Universal ratios give sharp targets, because their values do not depend on material details, only on the transition class.
arxiv-2512-03895:
Two fashionable ideas in machine learning, spiking networks and quantum circuits, are usually trained separately because spikes do not differentiate smoothly. Luu Trong Nhan and colleagues merge them into one trainable system in a 2025 neural computation preprint. Their SQDR-CNN, a spiking-quantum convolutional network using data re-uploading, trains a spiking encoder and a quantum circuit together in one backpropagation framework.

Earlier hybrid designs leaned on pre-trained spiking encoders and trimmed datasets. The new architecture needs neither shortcut and still converges to reasonable performance. They test design choices around quantum data re-uploading, training algorithms, and initialisation, including under noisy simulated quantum conditions. The model reached most of the accuracy of leading spiking baselines while using a tiny fraction of the parameters. The team hopes the integration opens fresh directions for learnable systems that mix neuromorphic and quantum parts.
arxiv-2512-04095:
Keeping a modern power grid stable as inverter-based renewables flood in requires fast, accurate security control, and the underlying equations are slow to solve. Amin Masoumi and Mert Korkali test a quantum-flavoured remedy in a 2025 systems preprint. Their framework embeds quantum computing elements inside a deep reinforcement learning controller for dynamic security control of the grid.

Model-free reinforcement learning already performs reliably here. It learns control policies without solving the full differential-algebraic system each time. The authors organise a hybrid version drawing on near-term, noisy quantum hardware concepts. They assess its dependability on the standard IEEE 39-bus test network. Results, they report, show promising applications alongside shortcomings they name openly. The paper is framed as groundwork: an organised framework and an honest evaluation, pointing at what to fix before quantum-embedded control can be trusted with a real grid.
arxiv-2512-04195:
Stars forge heavy elements slowly, one captured neutron at a time, and laboratory beams try to mimic that stellar furnace. Sarah Agus-Bina's 2025 master's thesis in experimental nuclear physics examines one candidate mimic: firing protons at oxygen-18 to release neutrons via fluorine-18. Earlier work showed its neutron spectrum near threshold closely resembles the thermal flux inside asymptotic giant branch stars.

The thesis repeats that experiment at PTB and builds a computational tool, OxyGen. The tool predicts the neutron energy spectrum and angular distribution for a planned liquid-water oxygen target at the SARAF facility. Those predictions feed into Geant4 transport simulations, which the author compares against the experimental results. The verdict is reassuring: OxyGen forecasts the spectrum reliably. Future SARAF experiments can therefore be planned and analysed with it at different proton energies.
arxiv-2512-04495:
Zhu-yao Jin and Jun Jing develop a general method to steer open quantum systems whose energy can leak or grow. Such systems are called non-Hermitian, and past control work copied tricks from closed systems by staring at energy spectra. That focus left time behavior and scale hard to handle. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds control in the Heisenberg picture instead, where operators carry the motion.

The method works for any number of bosonic modes under a Hamiltonian that changes with time. It rests on moving frames defined by helper operators mixed from the lab-frame ones. A gauge potential, born from the twist between frames, steers the dynamics. This view reaches far past states with a few excitations. It also stays workable as mode counts grow. The theory could guide control of light and sound modes in leaky quantum devices, where loss is a fact of life.
arxiv-2512-04695:
Jinglue Xu, Qi Sun, Peter Schwendeman, and co-authors present TRINITY, a small coordinator model that directs larger language models as a team. Merging model weights fails when architectures differ or APIs stay closed. A coordinator sidesteps both walls by delegating in words. Their 2025 arXiv paper trains a compact coordinator, well under a billion parameters, plus a tiny routing head, using an evolutionary strategy rather than gradient training.

Across several turns, the coordinator hands each query step to a chosen model in one of three roles: Thinker, Worker, or Verifier. Complex skill stays inside the big models; the coordinator only learns whom to ask and when. Tests across coding, math, reasoning, and domain knowledge show the team beating single models and prior routing methods. The approach also carried over to new model pools, a hint that cheap coordination can scale with the model market.
arxiv-2512-04895:
M. Zeeshan, Saud Satti, and co-authors present Chameleon, an attack framework that hides hostile instructions inside images where only machines can read them. Vision-language models now drive document processing and automated decisions. To save compute, their pipelines shrink incoming images by default. That innocent scaling step opens a hole: text invisible at full size can sharpen into clear instructions after downscaling. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows how adaptive agents can exploit the gap.

Older attacks are static, painted once for one pipeline. Chameleon instead adapts its hidden prompts to the workflow it faces, in the spirit of agentic systems themselves. The planted instructions wake only after the model's own preprocessing, slipping past human review of the original image. The work warns builders of multimodal systems to audit every resize and crop as a security surface, not a mere efficiency step.
arxiv-2512-04995:
Markus Meinert takes a fresh computational look at ruthenium dioxide, a metal oxide caught in an argument about magnetism. In perfect bulk form the material shows no magnetism, yet a popular calculation method predicts a special magnetic state called altermagnetism, and strained or doped thin films give mixed signals. Which answer is right depends heavily on the tools used to compute it.

Meinert reruns the calculations with a more advanced method that tracks extra detail about how electrons move and bunch up. The newer method strengthens the push toward magnetism but still finds the undisturbed material nonmagnetic at its measured size. Stretching the crystal, removing some electrons, or straining it along one axis, though, tips it into the magnetic state. The study sets cautious thresholds for how much distortion or doping that takes.
arxiv-2512-05595:
Tommaso Polonelli and five co-authors built a radar system that watches lab rodents without touching them. Checking heart and breathing rates in mice and rats usually means implants or wires, or picking the animals up. Their 2025 paper puts a low power radar beside the home cage. Working at sixty gigahertz, it reads tiny body motions from the echoes that bounce back.

The team tuned where the sensor sits and built a processing chain. It picks the right range slice, reads phase shifts, and pulls out breathing rates. In tests with two rodents, rates came out accurate to about two breaths per minute. The radar also tracks where each animal is and how it moves, sensing shifts as small as a few centimeters, even in group housing. Nothing is attached and no one handles the animals, so the setup promises calmer subjects and cleaner data, around the clock.
arxiv-2512-05695:
Chunyu Wang and Brian Tom write on learning the best sequence of treatments for a patient over time, known as a dynamic treatment regime. Precision medicine wants rules that say which treatment to give at each decision point, based on the patient's history. Clinicians prefer rules built from simple, readable models. But a simple model can miss the true pattern, and a late error feeds back into earlier estimates.

Their 2025 paper focuses on picking the model for the contrast functions that compare treatments. Because a model's rank can flip with sample size, they judge candidates by performance at the sample size actually in hand, not by far-off limits. They use a counterfactual cross-validation score, and add a new way to estimate its variance. Knowing the uncertainty lets researchers test whether a preferred simple structure is really supported. The result is model selection that admits its own doubt.
arxiv-2512-05995:
Ali Dasdan's working paper argues that two famous frustrations are the same failure. Productivity has risen roughly eightfold since Keynes predicted the fifteen hour week in 1930, yet people still work about twice those hours. AI development also races ahead despite stark warnings from its own leading researchers. Dasdan shows both are coordination failures with one game theoretic skeleton: rational choices producing worse outcomes together. Five conditions define such tragedies, from defection paying more to blocked enforcement.

The framework is validated on canonical cases, then sharpened with a Tragedy Index built from condition intensities. Governing transformative AI scores orders of magnitude harder than climate change or nuclear weapons. Applied to labor, firms cannot convert productivity gains into worker welfare under competition. The drone war in Ukraine appears as field evidence. Dasdan stops at naming the problem.
arxiv-2512-06295:
Angelina Mendoza Tavera, Adrian Escobar Ruiz, and Robin Sagar compare three ways of picturing a quantum state as it shifts from one well to two. Their test case is a special oscillator whose energy curve can be solved in part by hand, making it a clean lab. As a knob turns, its single dip splits into two dips, and a particle can tunnel between them.

The team draws each picture for the lowest states with high care: the Wigner view, a smoothed Husimi view, and a plain size only view of the first. Measures of spread and shared detail show a clear ranking. Only the Wigner view caught the wave like clash effects as the wells split, with a wavy pattern in its spread measures. The others saw only the split itself. The work gives a yardstick for picking the right picture when quantum states change shape.
arxiv-2512-06595:
Joe Shymanski presents ChargingBoul, an automated negotiator that nearly won its class at an international contest. Software agents that haggle over price and terms serve online markets, resource sharing, and machine to machine deals, where no human has time to bargain. In the twenty twenty two Automated Negotiating Agents Competition, ChargingBoul placed second on individual gain by an exceptionally narrow margin.

Its design is deliberately light. The agent sorts opponents into types by how their bids move, then tunes its own bidding to match. Early on it holds firm; late in the talks it shifts to a concession policy that trades a little gain for a higher chance of closing a deal. The study reviews its contest record and later uses of the agent in other research. ChargingBoul held up across many rival styles, and the author points to richer opponent modeling as the next step.
arxiv-2512-06695:
Haipeng Cao, Kaining Zhang, Dacheng Tao, and Zhaofeng Su unblock a quantum generative model that stalled as it grew. The quantum denoising diffusion model learns to build quantum states by reversing a noising process, and it has shown promise on correlated noise, many body phases, and topological data. The authors prove, and confirm in experiments, that a barren plateau appears as the system grows: the training signal flattens to nothing, so learning stops.

Their analysis pins the plateau on a cause distinct from the known ones for quantum circuits. They then redesign the architecture so the signal survives, restoring trainability in the settings tested. A conditional version of the fixed model can also generate ground states matched to given Hamiltonian parameters, widening its use for preparing complex quantum states. The work speaks to the wider problem of keeping quantum learning trainable at scale.
arxiv-2512-07395:
Alessandro Letti and co-authors keep fully powered machines safe while they move through space in the mathematically natural language of their motion. Their systems are mechanical and fully actuated, able to command every direction of movement, and their poses live on a Lie group, the smooth space of positions and orientations. Safety is enforced by zeroing control barrier functions, fences in the mathematics that the controller is forbidden to cross.

Two new families of such fences are introduced and proven sound. The first enforces kinematic constraints, the machinery behind obstacle avoidance. The second caps kinetic energy along chosen directions of translation and rotation. The relevant limit when a machine must touch its surroundings gently, as in safe physical interaction with people or fragile cargo. Computer simulations put the fences to work in two scenarios: slipping through a narrow slit, and landing safely.
arxiv-2512-07695:
Natalie Allen and twenty-six co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a nearby planetary system. TRAPPIST-1 hosts several small rocky planets, and one, planet e, sits at a temperate distance. Finding air on such a world is a flagship goal for exoplanet science.

The James Webb Space Telescope watches planet e cross its star. Starspots and other surface features contaminate those transit readings badly.  The team's program uses a clever partner: airless planet b. Its close transits trace the star's face without any atmosphere in the way. Those passes should let the team correct planet e's spectrum without a star model. Simulations say the planned set of close transits can reveal an Earth-like air. Early observations are reported here. Strong flares can spoil the trick by changing the star. The cleanest visit shows the correction working as hoped.
arxiv-2512-07795:
Nearchos Potamitis, Vansh Ramani, Har Ashish Arora, Dhairya Kuchhal, Lars Klein, and Akhil Arora wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Leaderboards for reasoning models report one score per system. Run the same system again, and the score, and the cost, can shift meaningfully.

That wobble is not mere noise to be averaged away. The top strategy beats its nearest rival in only about three runs out of four.  Their benchmark, ReasonBENCH, records many repeated trials for each contender. Ten strategies, a dozen models, and six tasks enter the design. Quality and cost are treated as distributions, not point values. A two-part taxonomy sorts the variance into global and run-level noise. Architecture, they find, predicts a strategy's stability profile. Most score variance traces to benchmark, system, and item structure. Cheap methods resist joint cost-quality failure; expensive ones stay exposed.
arxiv-2512-08095:
Miguel Alcubierre, Juan Barranco, Argelia Bernal, and colleagues, relativists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about clouds of scalar field gathered around black holes. These self gravitating clouds resemble atoms, with the black hole as nucleus. Earlier work built such gravitational atoms mainly without angular momentum structure.

The team presents new solutions of the Einstein Klein Gordon equations that include an angular momentum number. They call them noble gravitational atoms, by analogy with noble atoms and their closed electron shells. In the right limit, the solutions approach the known boson star family, differing only very near the horizon. For higher angular momentum, the density peaks can sit far from the hole, and the usual spike at the horizon may vanish or dip. Some of these objects could be as large as galaxies, as dilute as dark matter, and as long lived as the universe.
arxiv-2512-08295:
Neil Beri, John Palastro, Qian Qian, and colleagues, plasma physicists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about photon acceleration in a plasma wakefield. When a drive beam crosses a plasma, a laser pulse riding its wake can shift to much higher frequency, promising intense short wavelength light. Tailoring the plasma density keeps the pulse in step with the wake.

The team studies how photons move in phase space near that matching condition. A photon kinetic model, checked against full particle in cell simulations, supports a linear theory of the dynamics. The theory yields scaling laws for the witness pulse and a self similar solution for the photon pattern. One striking prediction says the pulse can be compressed without any lower bound on its duration. If borne out, photon acceleration could become a source of sub femtosecond, short wavelength radiation for probing ultrafast matter.
arxiv-2512-08495:
Michael Ling and Yang Yang, researchers in space dynamics, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about sorting low Earth orbit debris. When a satellite breaks up, its fragments form a family, and reconnecting those families supports space sustainability and awareness. Machine learning on proper elements, the stable fingerprints of an orbit, is a key tool, but models trained on old debris pictures may age badly.

The team builds a pipeline on synthetic breakups from a standard model, flown through a high fidelity simulation. They extract proper elements in three coordinate sets, widening the fingerprints a classifier can use. Neural networks then judge whether two fragments share a parent. One subtle trap surfaced: standard quaternion features lose orbital size data during normalization, wrecking accuracy until an augmented set restored it. With the joint feature sets, the best model clearly beat the single set baseline, sharpening automated debris genealogy.
arxiv-2512-08595:
Rohan Sarkar, a probabilist, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. He studies spectral heat content, a quantity that watches a random process wander inside a region and measures how much of it stays put. Its behavior at very small times encodes the geometry of the boundary.

Sarkar gives a new technique for deriving those small time asymptotics for a broad class of processes at once: any translation invariant, isotropic process whose far jumps are negligible. One proof thereby recovers several known results for Levy processes and Gaussian processes. It also yields new results for stable Levy processes whose clock is warped by a self similar process, linked to equations nonlocal in space and time. One method thus simplifies a scattered literature.
arxiv-2512-08695:
Rashmi Kamran and coauthors review a recent telecom standard that updates the design of next generation networks. Those networks underpin most wired and wireless packet based systems, including advanced mobile networks. A core design goal was to keep user services separate from the transport layer that carries them, so services would not depend on one transport technology.

In practice, that split was applied to outside services but not to internal ones such as mobility and authentication. Internal services stayed tied to transport control, forcing each transport to support them on its own and causing duplication. The new recommendation extends the split to internal services as well. The review explains the evolved design and why it is more modular and scalable, including as a template for future sixth generation networks.
arxiv-2512-09095:
Xinyue Pan, Yuhao Chen, Jiangpeng He, and Fengqing Zhu tackle a surprising failure in food image generation. A prompt such as egg noodle can yield an image with eggs and noodles as separate items, which is wrong. Such compound categories are common in real food data sets and form a large share of standard benchmarks.

The errors come from two sources. Text encoders lack knowledge tied to multi noun food categories, and models misread how the nouns relate, leading to wrong layouts. Their method, FoCULR, adds food domain knowledge and introduces core concepts early in the generation process. That early grounding helps the model treat the name as one dish rather than a list of ingredients. Experiments show the combined techniques improve generation quality in the food domain. The work highlights a broader lesson: compound names need explicit semantic handling,.
arxiv-2512-09195:
Antonio Ortiz, Dushmanta Sahu, and Gyula Bencedi examine a puzzle from proton-proton collisions studied by the ALICE experiment. When very few particles are produced, a long-range pattern still appears in the angles at which particles fly out. That pattern, measured by a quantity called V2Δ, is not yet understood at low particle counts.

The authors test one possible cause using a computer model called PYTHIA8 with an added mechanism known as string shoving, which can create the angular pattern. They check how the result changes with particle counts, the number of separate parton collisions, and a measure called flattenicity. String shoving matches the low-count limit best for the simplest collisions, but its pattern falls as particle counts rise, unlike the data. The team concludes that string shoving may explain the low end, while fluid-like behavior matters more when many particles are produced.
arxiv-2512-09395:
D. J. Fritzewski and colleagues measure how fast stars spin deep inside, using pulsations in members of the Pleiades star cluster. The Pleiades is a nearby cluster, but its gravity-mode pulsators, whose oscillations probe the core region, had never been analyzed. Such measurements reveal rotation on the main sequence, a key input for stellar evolution models.

Using images from the TESS telescope, the team built light curves for intermediate-mass members and searched for gravity-mode pulsations. Among about a hundred target stars they found twenty-eight pulsators, most of them hybrids showing two kinds of oscillation. Only three showed the spacing patterns that give the firmest rotation rates, but rates could be estimated for the rest from their main frequencies. Core rotation rates spread widely with no clear dependence on mass, a broader spread than in a similar cluster, though the two share a similar asteroseismic age.
arxiv-2512-09795:
Yuting Feng and colleagues measure how stars move in the outer halo of the Milky Way. They used the Keck II telescope to take spectra of fifty-five RR Lyrae stars, a pulsating type useful as a distance marker. The targets came from three sky surveys and lie far from the galactic center. From the spectra the team derived each star's radial velocity, its speed toward or away from us.

The spread of velocities came out at about seventy kilometers per second. The pattern hints at a lopsided structure, with the northern half shifted one way and the southern half the other. Fitting a model in which the Large Magellanic Cloud tugs on the halo gave only a weak signal, but the data fit a halo thrown out of balance by that galaxy. The study also caught ten supposed candidates that were distant quasars, a warning for image based surveys.
arxiv-2512-09895:
Jane Greenberg and a large team introduce MatSci-YAMZ, a platform that pairs artificial intelligence with human judgment to build metadata vocabularies. Such vocabularies support findable, reusable research data, but building them is slow because expert time is scarce. The platform lets an AI draft term definitions, then routes them through people, including crowdsourced contributors, who refine them in rounds of feedback. The test case is materials science, a field that borrows language from many disciplines.

In a proof of concept study, six participants from a national research institute used the platform over several weeks. They contributed definitions and examples that prompted the AI to revise its drafts. Nineteen AI generated definitions were completed this way. The authors count the trial a success, yielding a protocol others can follow, and argue the model could scale to other domains.
arxiv-2512-09995:
A team led by So Chigusa quantifies what future plasma wakefield colliders could discover among new electroweak particles. Wakefield machines speed up particles in plasma waves and could reach multi teraelectronvolt energies in compact sites. The targets are new particle multiplets carrying electroweak charge, a classic place for physics beyond the Standard Model to hide. A key snag is beam beam interaction, which smears the collision energy into a spectrum. The authors include realistic beam spectra and compare five machine designs, including electron positron, electron electron, and photon colliders with unlike beam shapes.

Beam effects change search plans versus idealized colliders. The low energy part of the spectrum and extra beam induced channels become important. Key electroweak targets may stay within reach even if positron acceleration and flat beam delivery, both hard in practice, do not pan out at these energies. That relaxes two risky demands for a future machine.
arxiv-2512-10095:
Jiachen Tao and colleagues present TraceFlow, a system for rendering moving scenes full of mirrors and shiny surfaces. Mirror-like reflections are where dynamic reconstruction usually breaks: reflection directions must be estimated with care, and the physics modeled honestly. Their method builds on two dimensional Gaussian splatting, topped up with residual material data, so dynamic geometry and material traits support accurate reflection rays. A dynamic environment Gaussian captures the surroundings that reflections sample. Rendering then splits into diffuse and specular parts.

The shiny part is made with real ray tracing, while the diffuse part uses fast rasterization. A coarse to fine training plan steadies the fitting and encourages a physically meaningful split between the two parts. On dynamic scene benchmarks, it beat prior methods on both measured scores and visual quality. Reflections came out sharper and truer in complex moving scenes.
arxiv-2512-10595:
Maximillian Fainkich, Kiril Solovey, and Anna Clarke plan safer landings for human-piloted parafoils, the steerable parachutes used in skydiving. Most skydiving accidents happen during piloting and landing, through lapses of judgement. Yet training is slow because good simulators are scarce and little work exists on computing safe flight paths a trainee could follow.

The team adapted a sampling-based planner, Stable Sparse RRT, to the parafoil's constraints, treating low bank angle as a stand-in for safety. Against recorded human flights, the planner's routes cost far less, improving on the pilots by a wide margin. Humans tended to rush toward the landing spot, then spiral down to shed height. The algorithm instead descends smoothly and gradually, arriving at exactly the height needed for final approach, evidence that computed guidelines could anchor future training simulators.
arxiv-2512-10795:
Anna Tsai, Dylan Jow, and Ue-Li Pen show how pulsar timing arrays could reach their sharpest possible vision. These arrays time an ensemble of pulsars to detect gravitational-wave sources, but standard analyses underuse the pulsars' distances, giving up angular resolution and perhaps half the detection sensitivity. Distance is the missing coordinate that turns arrival times into a map.

Their coherent map-making technique folds precise pulsar distances into the analysis. It reaches the diffraction limit, the finest resolution the array's size allows. For a strong source, that means a patch of sky only a couple of arcminutes wide. At a signal-to-noise ratio of ten, roughly today's coherent reach, about nine measured pulsars suffice. Each added pulsar with an accurate distance sharpens the picture steeply. And the best-timed millisecond pulsar already has a sub-parsec distance. So the authors argue the coherent analysis is timely now.
arxiv-2512-10995:
Muhammad Usamah Shahid and Muddassar Farooq build models that predict when a chemotherapy plan is likely to fail or be stopped early. Long cancer treatments bring physical, financial, and emotional costs, so early warning matters for patients and families. Their data come from real patient records held in an oncology electronic health system.

The team built feature sets from clinical notes, diagnoses, and medicines, focusing on five cancer types with frequent treatment failures. They compared model designs along three lines: accuracy, complexity, and how well doctors can understand the result. Boosted random forests won that balance, giving solid accuracy while staying simple enough for oncologists to use and trust in practice.
arxiv-2512-11295:
Nattaya Mairittha, Gabriel Phorncharoenmusikul, and Sorawit Worapradidth propose a number that exposes AI products secretly powered by human labour. Some vendors market human in the loop systems as automated while workers invisibly perform the core tasks, a pattern the authors call human instead of AI. They argue such designs are ethically troubling and economically unsustainable.

Their AI Autonomy Coefficient measures the share of tasks a system completes without mandatory human intervention. A companion deployment algorithm acts as a gate, requiring a minimum autonomy score during offline testing and shadow running before launch. In their results the coefficient flagged deceptive systems with low scores, while systems built under their AI first, human empowered framework scored far higher. The authors present the metric as a practical tool for transparency and honest automation claims.
arxiv-2601-06695:
Sphiwe Skhosana and Weixin Yao build a sturdier mix model for grouped data in a 2026 paper. Mix models sort data into hid groups, each with its own trend line. Loose forms let those trends bend with the inputs in free ways.

Those loose forms lean on a bell shape for their noise, though. That makes their fits jumpy when wild points show up in the data. Thick tails in the noise also break their care in real use. Their fix adds a tainted bell part that soaks up wild points. The loose parts keep the bend that made mix models prized at first. The mix thus bends without breaking when data turn rough or wild. The model suits grouped data where extremes are the norm, not the rare case.
arxiv-2601-06895:
A 2026 arXiv paper in pure math gives exact values for a class of Euler sums. Euler sums are sums built from harmonic numbers, which add up the parts one over one, one over two, and so on. Here the sums also use parts with fractions, not whole steps alone. The paper treats two such sums side by side.

In one sum, each term pairs a harmonic number with a power term. In the next, the signs of the terms switch from plus to minus as the sum goes on. Three whole-number inputs steer both sums. One input must not equal one. For readers in number theory, the paper gives closed forms where past work had sums with no short form. Such forms let readers check and reuse the sums with care.
arxiv-2601-07095:
Research by Tadashi Wadayama and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with Score-Based VAMP with Fisher-Information-Based onsager correction. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors propose score-based VAMP (SC-VAMP). A variant of vector approximate message passing (VAMP) in which the Onsager correction is expressed and computed via conditional Fisher information. Thereby enabling a Jacobian-free implementation.

Using learned score functions, SC-VAMP constructs nonlinear minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimators through Tweedie’s formula and derives. The corresponding Onsager terms from the score-norm statistics. Avoiding the need for analytical derivatives of the prior or likelihood. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07495:
L. I. Danilov studies the spectrum of a charged particle in a magnetic field, in this 2026 mathematics and physics preprint. The model is the Landau Hamiltonian with an added periodic electric potential. Landau Hamiltonians describe electrons moving under a steady magnetic field. Their energy levels are a classic subject in quantum mechanics.

Danilov proves that, for every natural number m, special periodic potentials exist with certain spectral behavior. The potentials he constructs are smooth, nonconstant, and have zero mean value. They depend analytically on a small parameter. The result concerns what happens near a chosen Landau level. Readers in mathematical physics get a precise statement about how a periodic electric field can reshape magnetic energy levels.
arxiv-2601-07595:
A large IceCube and gravitational wave collaboration searches for cosmic events that emit both neutrinos and gravitational waves. Joint sources have been a primary target for LIGO, Virgo, KAGRA, and IceCube. Finding one would reveal processes that neither signal shows alone. The search uses data from the third observing run of LIGO and Virgo. Their 2026 preprint describes a deep search of that data.

High-energy neutrinos point back to violent cosmic accelerators. Gravitational waves reveal mergers and collapses of compact objects. A joint detection could connect the two pictures for the same event. The authors note targets from compact object mergers to relativistic outflows. Even a careful non-detection sets useful limits. Multi-messenger astronomers use such searches to plan the next observing runs.
arxiv-2601-07695:
A 2026 preprint tackles a weak point of vision-language models: giving exact numbers for three-dimensional scenes. Precise numerical prediction is a bottleneck for 3D scene understanding. Traditional reinforcement learning for this task ranks answers against each other. That relative approach often suffers sparse rewards and unstable gradients. It also fails to use the checkable signals that 3D physical constraints provide.

The authors propose a smooth verifiable reward, presented under the name Smooth Operator. Verifiable rewards pay the model only when an answer can be checked as right. Smoothing that signal aims to keep training stable while staying honest. Better spatial numbers would help robots and assistants judge distance, size, and position. The paper targets scholars training vision-language models for grounded spatial reasoning.
arxiv-2601-07995:
Laurits Lyngbaek and coauthors ask whether the shape of sentiment in language models curves like a banana. Work in the humanities often needs sentiment scores set in context, on a smooth scale. Concept vector projections treat sentiment as a direction in embedding space. They give smooth scores in more than one language that match human judgments with care. How well the method moves to new fields, and what it takes for granted, are still not well probed. Their 2026 preprint probes both points.

If that direction bends, a straight line read will misread texts at the far ends. Testing the shape tests the method's foundations. How well it moves decides whether scholars can trust scores on new kinds of text. The authors span computational linguistics and digital humanities groups in Denmark. The paper serves scholars who apply sentiment tools to cultural material. It checks the ruler before measuring with it.
arxiv-2601-08295:
Gregor Autischer, Kerstin Waxnegger, and Dominik Kowald test self-certification for high-risk AI systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper takes facial emotion recognition as the working example. The European Union AI Act sets broad duties for high-risk systems, but harmonized standards remain incomplete.

The team applies the Fraunhofer AI assessment catalogue as a certification framework. They run a complete self-certification cycle on the emotion recognition system. That full pass shows where catalogue checks work in practice and where gaps stay open. For compliance teams, the study offers a concrete rehearsal of duties that will soon be enforced across Europe.
arxiv-2601-08495: A. Conta and four co-authors present a toolchain for shuttling trapped-ion qubits in segmented traps. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that scalable trapped-ion computing needs fast, reliable ion transport. Ions must move through complex segmented radiofrequency trap architectures without excess motional excitation. Extra motion heats the ions and degrades gate quality. The toolchain generates time-dependent electrode voltages for fast, low-excitation shuttling in a systematic way. Reliable shuttling is a building block for larger trapped-ion processors with many zones.
arxiv-2601-09095:
Yin-Fa Shen and four co-authors plan a hunt for heavy neutrinos at the Large Hadron Collider. A neutrino is a near ghost bit that skims through stuff. A heavy form could solve open asks on why plain neutrinos weigh so slight. Past hunts rest on plain links of the heavy form to known bits. This team lets those links vary by bit type.

They add a new make path at the lab and sharp learn tools to pick its trace. The trace is a charged bit, lost push, and two jets of spray. A reader in core physics gets a hunt that can reach zones past hunts left blind.
arxiv-2601-09395:
Ricardo Mamede, José Luis Santos, and Diogo Soares count special spellings of permutations. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies reduced words, the shortest ways to write a permutation as a product of simple swaps. A commutation class groups spellings that differ only by swapping distant, commuting swaps.

The authors bound the number of one-element commutation classes, classes whose spelling admits no commutation at all. From that bound they prove a conjecture linking the number of reduced words to the number of commutation classes. Counts like these sit at the heart of Coxeter group theory and Schubert calculus. The result tightens what is known about how permutations can be spelled.
arxiv-2601-09695:
Michael Konstantinou, Renzo Degiovanni, and Mike Papadakis check whether newer language models write better unit tests. Their 2026 arXiv paper revisits LLM-based test generation as models evolve. Automated test generation is a growing use of language models in software engineering.

Used alone, models produce many tests that fail to compile or cover little code. The authors ask how much newer model versions improve that record. The answer tells teams whether to upgrade models, add post-processing, or both. Test generation only saves effort if the tests run and actually exercise the code.
arxiv-2601-09795:
Lucas Michel builds counterexamples in a theory used to carve space into simple cells. His 2026 arXiv paper constructs exotic cylindrical algebraic decompositions and cells. Such decompositions, enriched with topological properties, serve logic, algorithm design, and robot motion planning.

They also help study the topology of semi-algebraic sets. Michel gives explicit examples that refute several conjectures and open questions of J. H. Davenport and others. Counterexamples prune false hopes from the map of a theory like this one. They show exactly which nice properties a decomposition of this kind cannot always have in practice.
arxiv-2601-09895:
Connor Quinn proves bounds for a wave flow on a square torus. The flow tracks how a wave spreads in time and space. Bounds of Strichartz type say how much the wave can pile up. Quinn works at the key power where such bounds are most hard to get.

He shows the bound holds with no loss. The wave starts with its tones in a fixed band. The time span is short, and its length rests on the tone size. Sharp bounds with no loss are prized in wave work. On closed spaces, some loss is the norm, so a clean bound stands out.
arxiv-2601-09995:
Masahito Hayashi and Jinpei Zhao bring a classic tool into quantum work. In classic stats, a chain of linked vars can split in two ways at once. This trait is named double Markovity. It backs proofs that Gauss forms are best for some tasks.

The pair prove a quantum form of the trait. They work with states split in three parts. Two chain forms can hold at once. When they do, set tests on two parts yield one shared label. That label splits the first part from the pair. The result opens a path to quantum forms of those best form proofs.
arxiv-2601-10095:
Yuda Li, Shaoyuan Li, and Xiang Yin work out which states can reach a goal in a timed net. Such nets model lines where steps must sync and waits stack. They are named max plus linear systems. The math tracks the worst link in a chain.

The team looks back in time. They seek all states that can hit a goal set in a set count of steps. They use shape tools named polyhedra to mark those states. Sharp marks of this kind help plan lines and check them. They show if a line can meet a due time from a given start.
arxiv-2601-10695:
Sriram Ganeshan and Alan T. Dorsey bring quantum geometry to a classic model of the air and sea. The rotating shallow water equations drive much of weather and ocean modeling. Their waves also mirror waves in electron gases and active fluids. Recent work stressed the topology of these wave bands, their global twists.

The authors build the complementary view, computing the full quantum geometric tensor for the linearized model on a rotating plane. That tensor captures how wave states change shape across the band. It can reveal forces and drifts that topology alone misses. The work links geophysical flows to ideas from modern condensed matter physics.
arxiv-2601-10795:
A Euclid Collaboration paper takes up weak lensing, the slight bending of galaxy images by gravity. Surveys that use lensing must correct for the point spread function, the blur of the telescope itself. For a space telescope, that blur is diffraction-limited. The correction depends on each galaxy's spectral energy distribution, its color profile across wavelengths.

So every galaxy in the survey needs a well-known spectrum before its shape can be trusted. The paper works through that requirement for Euclid. Small shape errors, summed over millions of galaxies, could fake or hide dark matter signals. The study is part of the careful groundwork that makes lensing maps believable.
arxiv-2601-10895:
Chunhui Liu bounds the rational points that conics can supply on a cubic surface. A cubic surface is a shape cut out by a degree-three equation. Its rational points, solutions with whole-number ratios, are a classic topic in number theory. Conics lying on the surface can carry many such points, so counting them needs care.

Liu gives a uniform upper bound on the rational points of bounded height that these conics provide. The proof generalizes Salberger's global determinant method through Arakelov geometry. Uniform bounds matter because they hold across families, not just for one surface. The result feeds the long effort to say how many rational points a shape can hold.
arxiv-2601-11195:
Jiaming Huang and Luca Neri work on a core task in applied economics here. Their 2026 preprint deals with SVAR models, used to trace shocks. A key step is to name the shocks with proxy variables. In real work, teams face a zoo of such proxies to pick from.

Most past frames ask for exact exogeneity from the proxy. That is, the proxy must link to one shock and no others. Huang and Neri drop that strict demand in their frame. They use ranking bounds on how proxies link to shocks. A smooth quality score sets how much slack each proxy gets. The frame aims at claims that hold up when proxies are flawed.
arxiv-2601-11295:
Kareem Abdelmaqsoud and four coauthors design tungsten alloys on a computer. Their 2026 preprint seeks alloys that bend rather than snap. Tungsten stands heat and radiation better than most metals. That makes it a top pick for harsh spots like fusion reactors.

The flaw of tungsten is that it is brittle by nature. It is also hard to print with additive methods. Printing gives free shapes and fast prototype runs for parts. A ductile, printable tungsten alloy would unlock those gains. The team's design work is done in silico, by computation. It hunts mixes that keep the strengths and lose the brittleness.
arxiv-2601-11395:
Alberto Dominguez Corella and Onesimo Hernandez-Lerma prove a maximum principle for control. Their 2026 preprint covers discrete-time systems and dynamic games. Optimal control in discrete time steps drives many models. The systems here are deterministic and can shift over time.

The team treats both finite and infinite time horizons. With Gateaux differentials, they prove a discrete maximum principle. It stands next to the known continuous-time version. A transversality condition joins it as a needed condition. The pair is necessary for any optimal control path. Under extra assumptions, the pair is also sufficient. The team then applies the result to dynamic games. Games add rivals whose moves shape each player's best plan.
arxiv-2601-11495:
Hlel Missaoui proves global regularity for Musielak-Orlicz equations in this work. The 2026 preprint deals with elliptic equations in divergence form. Solutions gain C1-alpha regularity across the whole domain here. That means gradients exist and vary in a controlled way.

The equations have Musielak-Orlicz growth, a flexible general form. Boundary conditions can be Dirichlet or Neumann in the results. Bounded generalized solutions are the class covered by the work. The findings extend several known regularity results at once. Special cases include variable exponent spaces, a hot topic. Orlicz spaces and mixed p-q growth cases also fall out. One theorem thus covers many growth laws used in practice.
arxiv-2601-11895:
Pareesa Ameneh Golnari, Adarsh Kumarappan, Wen Wen, and their co-authors built a code test set from real developer data. The set, DevBench, holds 1,800 tasks in six code tongues and six task kinds. The tasks come from real telemetry, such as API use and code purpose.

Most code tests use toy tasks cut off from real work. A set drawn from real use can grade models on what devs truly do. It can also show which task kinds still trip models up. The work gives a shared scale for code models in real settings.
arxiv-2601-11995:
Donghuo Zeng, Hao Niu, Yanan Wang, and Masato Taya learn joint traits for sound and image clips. Clips that truly match should sit close in the trait space. Chance pairs, such as background noise or off-screen events, should not.

Most past tools use sparse labels and treat each joint clip as a true match. That bakes in noise. The team infer a latent graph of links between sound and image parts. A graph-led trait could be more clean for search and tagging of video.  Cleaner traits should lift search and tag scores for clips.
arxiv-2601-12195:
Nathaniel Gallup and Leo Gray prove a ring tied to intervals in the Bruhat order is Cohen-Macaulay. The group is the infinite symmetric group, all bijections of the whole numbers. Its Bruhat order sorts group terms by a known rule.

They study the order complex of set intervals in that order. Its Stanley-Reisner ring is non-Noetherian, so the claim needs a form for ideals and weak unmixedness. Cohen-Macaulay rings have tidy depth traits. The result links combinatorics of the infinite group to algebra.  The ring is built from the order complex of the intervals.
arxiv-2601-12695:
Hiroshi Okajima, Shun Shirahama, Tatsunori Hayashi, and Nobutomo Matsunaga work on system identification under noise. Model based control needs accurate mathematical models to guarantee performance and stability. Process and sensor noise make such models hard to obtain in practice. The team propose an algorithm that derives polytopic uncertainty models instead of one fixed model.

Their idea treats noise induced parameter swings as intrinsic uncertainty. A polytope then bounds the set of models that fit the data. The construction is systematic and uses a cyclic reformulation, per the title. A bounded set of models lets control design plan for the worst case inside it. That yields safer controllers for noisy real plants.
arxiv-2601-12895:
Chan Naseeb and five co authors build a deep learning system to guard identity documents. Generative AI models have escalated the threat of synthetic manipulation of ID documents. Face swapping and text inpainting attacks can fake a document with care. A fake that passes visual checks threatens banks, borders, and online verification.

Their architecture is called TwoHead-SwinFPN. It performs binary classification and precise localization of manipulated regions at the same time. Two heads share one backbone, so detection and localization inform each other. Knowing where a forgery sits helps human reviewers trust the verdict. Unified systems like this could harden document checks against AI era fraud.
arxiv-2601-13295:
Arpandeep Khatua and co-authors test if AI coding agents can act as teammates yet. To fix a team clash takes more than task skill. It takes social sense, the skill to find shared ground and build a deal all can take. As agents do more joint work, they need that same sense.

The team built a bench called CooperBench to test it. They start from a claim that today's agents lack such skills. Agents may each do fine solo work yet fail to mesh. The bench puts them in joint code tasks where they must sort clashes to pass. For agent builders, the gap it shows is a to do list, not just a score.
arxiv-2601-13395:
Andrew Zheng and Adam R. Stinchcombe grow the adjoint method to costs that are not holomorphic. The adjoint method is a fast way to get gradients in opt tasks with binds. It was built for real valued tasks whose parts split in the standard way. With complex values, as in radio and signal work, costs can fail that split.

Such costs are called non holomorphic. They are not differentiable in the standard sense. The pair give a broad adjoint form that can still yield gradients for them. That opens fast opt to a class of inverse tasks in electromagnetics and signal work that the old form could not serve.
arxiv-2601-13495:
J. Ferrer Asensio and co-authors track a small ring molecule and its heavy twins toward cold cores in the Perseus cloud. In such cores, cold and freeze out of carbon monoxide make heavy swaps fast. The molecule is cyclopropenylidene, a three carbon ring made early in chem growth. Its heavy forms tag gas phase heavy swap in such zones.

The cores span prestellar cores, on the edge of star birth, and starless cores with no star yet. By read of the ring and its twins in both kinds, the team can set how far heavy swap has run. That stage marks the clock of a core on its way to a star.
arxiv-2601-14095:
Babak Miraftab, Pat Morin, and Yelena Yuditsky link two measures of graph complexity in 2026. The basis number of a graph counts how edge cycles can be based on few sets. Pathwidth measures how close a graph is to a simple path in structure. The team proves two results relating the basis number to path decompositions.

Their first result shows the basis number is at most four times the pathwidth. A bound like this lets one measure stand in for an other. Graph measures guide algorithm design for networks, maps, and circuits. Firm links between them simplify many proofs.
arxiv-2601-14195:
Frederik Glitzner and David Manlove study matchings that are almost stable, from a minimax angle in 2026. Stability is crucial in matching markets, from hospital residency allocations to roommate assignments. In many real settings, full stability is impossible to achieve. Or it can come at the cost of leaving many agents unmatched.

Almost-stable matchings relax the stability demand in a controlled way. A minimax view minimizes the worst instability any agent faces. A preliminary version appears at AAMAS 2026. Better near-stable rules could fill more posts while keeping disputes low.
arxiv-2601-14395:
Daxal H. Mehta, John A. Regan, and Lewis Prole study the growth of light seed black holes in this 2026 paper. Light seeds form at the end point of the first generation of Population III stars. Those were the first stars in the early universe. The seeds appear as early as redshift 30 to 40, in low-mass dark matter halos.

The open question is how such small seeds grow. To become the giants seen later, they must gain mass fast in a young, harsh setting. The paper follows that growth problem. Readers get a study of one seed path for early black holes, set against the tight time the early universe allows.
arxiv-2601-14595:
Qiyue Mei and Michael Fu build a security analyzer for cloud scripts in this 2026 paper. Infrastructure as Code lets teams provision large-scale cloud and on-premise environments automatically. It cuts repetitive manual setup. The automation is a double-edged sword, though. A single misconfiguration in an IaC script can propagate widely, leading to severe downtime and security risks.

Their tool, IntelliSA, is an intelligent static analyzer for IaC security smell detection. A security smell is a pattern that hints at a flaw, even if it is not yet an exploit. The analyzer combines symbolic rules with neural inference. The read is plain. It shows how one bad line in a script can open a hole in a whole cloud. Readers get a checker that reads deployment scripts the way auditors wish they could.
arxiv-2601-14895:
Xinyi Zheng, Yunze Liu, and a team of co-authors build a memory system for machines that move through space. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents SpatialMem. The system stores a scene as one single record that a machine can search.

The record joins three kinds of data. It holds the 3D shape of a place, the meaning of what is in it, and words that name those things. Metric anchoring ties the record to true measured positions. Fast retrieval lets the system pull stored facts back at speed whenever a query asks for them.
arxiv-2601-14995:
Mojuan Yin, Ruohui Wang, Rui Zhou, Xueguang Qiao, and Shougang Zhang build a new way to sense tiny shaking through optical fiber. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with fiber-optic vibration sensors. Such sensors are weak at very low frequencies, the slow end of shaking.

The team uses an optical lattice clock, tuned by a method called Floquet engineering. Shaking in the wound fiber shifts the light's phase. The clock's tuned spectra read that shift out. The goal is to keep the sensor sharp from 200 hertz all the way down to near zero.
arxiv-2601-15095:
Biman Bagchi studies how stiff chain molecules fold up in a poor solvent. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with semiflexible polymers. In a poor solvent the chains collapse, and they can form globules, toroids, or rodlike bundles.

Two forces compete to shape the result. Attractive forces pull the chain inward, while stiffness resists bending. Simulations and experiments on stiff and conjugated polymers show complex crossovers between shapes. What is still missing is one single unified theory of those shape changes. Bagchi works steadily toward that missing unified account of the crossovers.
arxiv-2601-15195:
Ramtin Ehsani, Sakshi Pathak, and co-authors study what happens when AI coding agents submit work to real projects. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with pull requests on GitHub. Agents now act as contributors in their own right, not just as helpers at a human's side.

Agentic contributions are rising fast across real repositories. Yet many of these pull requests fail to be merged, and little is known about why. The authors run an empirical study of the failed ones. They sort the failure modes so builders can see where agents go wrong.
arxiv-2601-15295:
Yi Wang, John Joon Young Chung, and co-authors build a tool for writing interactive stories with AI. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with interactive narrative. Authors craft a space of possible story paths, and the player's input picks which path becomes real.

Generative AI can improvise fresh content inside that space as the player acts. The authors present Elsewise, an authoring tool for this kind of work. It shows the possibility space as a visual map. Writers can see the branches their story offers and where the AI may take them.
arxiv-2601-15395:
Tamunotonye Harry, Ivoline Ngong, and co-authors argue that a user's momentary state beats their fixed traits. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how people interact with language models. Interactions vary with who the user is, and with the context of the moment.

Existing persona datasets capture only the fixed traits. They ignore state, the pressure of the situation at hand. The authors introduce Chameleon, a dataset of contextual psychological profiles. It covers thousands of profiles from Reddit users, each measured across multiple contexts, so the role of state can finally be studied.
arxiv-2601-15795:
Erick Gushiken and Tetsuo Hyodo study near-threshold states in hadron physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Near a threshold, a bound state can turn into a resonance. Mass scaling describes how its mass moves during that change. Decay channels complicate the picture. The authors ask how decay affects the scaling. They use potential models to isolate the effect.

One model varies the strength of a square-well potential. It traces the pole trajectory as a bound state becomes a resonance. Decay enters in two ways. A single-channel complex potential handles it simply. A coupled-channel real potential handles it in more detail. Comparing the two shows which effects are real and which are model artifacts. Such care matters for reading exotic hadron signals.
arxiv-2601-15895:
Anne Arzberger, Enrico Liscio, and co-authors reframe AI alignment as a shared practice in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI systems now sit inside everyday work. Value misalignment has become a pressing concern. Mainstream alignment work stays model-centric, they argue. It treats users as passive recipients of preset values. Users are better seen as epistemic agents. They meet misalignment during real interactions and respond to it.

The authors draw on situated perspectives. Alignment, in their view, is co-constructed in human-AI interaction. The title names their participatory approach to situating AI values. That means values get worked out where systems are used, with the people affected. For design teams, the shift is practical: build ways for users to surface and negotiate value conflicts.
arxiv-2601-16395:
Sánchez-Salcedo sums the wake of a mass that moves through a flat gas layer. His 2026 preprint deals with the Bondi Hoyle Lyttleton flow. That flow is the wake left by a mass in a gas stream. Here the gas sits in a layer with a set height scale. The mass sits in the mid plane of that layer.
