balzac-colonel-chabert-marriage-1895:
Colonel Chabert was left for dead on the field of Eylau, buried under corpses, yet he lived. Balzac's short novel, in Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell's 1895 version, follows his return to Paris. His wife has married again and holds his fortune, and the law sees no easy way to raise a dead man.

A young lawyer takes the case, and pity fights paperwork through the tale. Chabert's end ranks among the saddest in the Human Comedy, a whole epic of war and loss in miniature. Many readers call it Balzac's most perfect short work, proof of how much he could hold in few pages.
balzac-country-doctor-marriage-1895:
Doctor Benassis arrives in a poor Savoy village and quietly rebuilds it, road by road and field by field. The Country Doctor, translated by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell in 1895, is Balzac's most hopeful provincial novel. It answers his Paris books, where greed rules, with a tale of patient public good.

Through talks with soldiers, peasants, and a dying water-carrier's son, Benassis shares his creed of work and order. His own buried sorrow explains the zeal that drives him. The novel, Le Médecin de campagne in French, remains the Human Comedy's great statement of what one devoted life can mend.
balzac-cousin-pons-marriage-1895:
Sylvain Pons loves music and old art, and asks little from life but meals at his cousins' table. Cousin Pons, in Ellen Marriage's 1895 translation, shows what happens when his quiet collection of pictures and curios gains real value. Relatives who once mocked him turn hunters, and the kind man has no defense ready.

Paired with Cousin Bette as Les Parents pauvres, the poor relations, this is among Balzac's darkest late novels. Greed works here through lawyers, dealers, and family duty, all smiling as they close in. Pons and his friend Schmucke stand as two innocents in a Paris that prices everything, even loyalty.
balzac-lost-illusions-marriage-1895:
Lucien de Rubempré leaves his small town for Paris with a poet's hopes, and Balzac's Lost Illusions tracks what the city does to him. Ellen Marriage's 1895 English version holds all three parts of the novel. At its heart stands the world of newspapers, where praise and ruin are both for sale.

Balzac shows printing shops, paper mills, and newsrooms as one great machine for grinding reputations. Lucien learns its rules too late, at a cost to everyone near him. Readers rank the book at the center of the Human Comedy, Balzac's vast portrait of French life after Napoleon.
balzac-magic-skin-marriage-1895:
A young man finds a strange piece of skin in a Paris antique shop, and The Magic Skin grants him every wish. Each wish, though, shrinks the skin, and with it his remaining life. Balzac's tale, La Peau de chagrin, made his name and anchors the thoughtful side of the Human Comedy.

Ellen Marriage translated the novel in 1895, and her version keeps its mix of wild fancy and sharp Paris detail. The hero must choose between wanting and living, a bargain no wealth can soften. Few novels state Balzac's great theme so cleanly: desire itself spends the life it feeds on.
balzac-pere-goriot-marriage-1895:
Honoré de Balzac wrote Father Goriot in French, and Ellen Marriage made it English in 1895. Marriage's version served J. M. Dent's landmark full Comédie Humaine in English dress. The novel of Parisian ambition sits near the heart of Balzac's vast human comedy.

Old Goriot, a rich pasta maker ruined by his daughters' greed, fades in a boarding house. Young Rastignac, a law student, learns Paris ways from the smooth rogue Vautrin there. Goriot dies calling for daughters who send empty carriages to his pauper's grave in Paris. Rastignac buries him and turns to face the city he vows to conquer next. Balzac maps money, rank, and family love with a surgeon's cold, clear eye.
balzac-the-thirteen-wormeley-marriage-18:
Thirteen men, bound by a secret pact, move through Balzac's Paris like a hidden government. The Thirteen gathers three tales, Ferragus, The Duchess of Langeais, and The Girl with the Golden Eyes, in the 1895 Wormeley and Marriage translations. Each story tests what the brotherhood will do for one of its own.

Love, kidnapping, and revenge drive the plots, while the thirteen hover at the edges, rich and unseen. Balzac gives his Human Comedy a conspiratorial heart here, a Paris beneath Paris. The trilogy mixes melodrama with his usual sharp eye for money, rank, and desire.
bekker-world-bewitched-1695:
Balthasar Bekker strikes at the Devil's power in The World Bewitch'd, in English from 1695. Bekker was a church man in Holland who used the new thought of Descartes. Spirits, he holds, can't push flesh: a soul with no bulk can't move a chair, sign a pact, or ride a broom through the night sky of his cold north land.

His four books take on witch trials, ghosts, and the Good Book's own tales. The church cast him out for it, yet his case spread. The book is a chief blow that broke the hunts. Its nerve still awes.
beowulf-morris-wyatt-1895:
William Morris and A. J. Wyatt gave English readers a new Beowulf in 1895, in the fine Kelmscott Press edition. Their text turns the Old English epic into rich, old-style verse. Beowulf, a hero from Geatland, sails to Denmark to help King Hrothgar.

Grendel, his mother, and a dragon that guards a hoard give the hero three great fights. The last fight costs Beowulf his life, and his people mourn a brave king. Morris loved old tales and fine books, and his version feels like both. It links the medieval poem to modern readers. Scholars still use it to feel the poem's rough music.
bibliographical-notes-on-histories-of-in: Bibliographical Notes on Histories of Inventions and Books of Secrets, 1895. The six papers. This book preserves that bibliography. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Its place in history is secure.
blavatsky-modern-panarion-1895:
Scraps and short tracts by H. P. Blavatsky fill A Modern Panarion, a set put out in 1895, past her death. She wrote for small tracts and weeklies through her career. Much of that work was hard to find. This set saves the best of it in one place.

Her voice here is sharp and game for a fight. She defends her creed, mocks its foes, and glosses hard points in brief. The set rounds out the shelf of her main books. It shows the fierce hand that built a world wide creed. The name Panarion comes from a saint's chest of cures for false creeds. Blavatsky's heirs chose it to claim her scraps held like worth.
brain-and-mind-or-mental-science-conside: Brain and Mind, 1895. The mental science. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
chaldean-oracles-westcott-1895:
William Wynn Westcott edited the Chaldaean Oracles of Zoroaster for English readers in 1895. The Oracles are fragments of Greek verse preserved by Neoplatonic philosophers. Tradition ascribed them to Zoroaster, though they date from the Roman era.

The fragments teach theurgy, the ritual work of rising toward the divine. Fire, the father, and the soul's ascent dominate the surviving lines. Neoplatonists prized these sayings above almost all other texts. Westcott gathered them with commentary for the occult revival's students. His edition overlaps his Collectanea Hermetica volume on the same text. The double publication shows how central the Oracles were to Golden Dawn teaching.
chambers-king-in-yellow-1895:
A banned play drives men mad in Robert W. Chambers's set of tales The King in Yellow, from 1895. Those who read the play see a pale king and a drowned city. Some tales share that lore. Some turn to love and art in Paris.

The first tales made the book's fame. Their hints of a vast, cruel myth drew praise from Lovecraft. He took the Yellow Sign for his own tales. The book still lures fans of weird lore and dread hints. Hastur, Carcosa, and the Lake of Hali haunt the tales as names half grasped. Those hints let each fan build the myth in their own mind.
cia-0000010595:
The Kashmir dispute's probable course to the end of 1951 is forecast in an August 1951 CIA estimate. India and Pakistan had fought their first war over the Himalayan state in 1947 and 1948. A ceasefire line divided it, and a promised vote on its future never came.

The estimate weighs talks, troop moves, and the young United Nations' role in the quarrel. Kashmir mattered because two new nations armed against each other over it. The dispute outlived every forecast made about it, including this one. The file preserves the quarrel's early shape, when many still expected a settlement.
cia-0000012295:
How the new Defense Intelligence Agency would be organized occupies a Helms memo to its director from November 1961. The subject line names the organizational structure under discussion. With the Penkovsky product flowing, the question of who inside the Pentagon would receive it, grade it, and act on it was anything but clerical.

The memo continues the steady exchange between Langley and the new agency through the busy autumn. It shows institution-building done under pressure, with a live case as the test. For readers, it reveals the plumbing behind intelligence: the boxes and lines that decided where secrets landed.
cia-0000012395:
Meeting number five, again in Leeds, falls on April 24, 1961, and its record carries a note of the pages it preserves. The Yorkshire sessions ran day after day that spring. Penkovsky's revelations accumulated with each sitting, as handlers worked through his knowledge of Soviet missiles, plans, and personalities in the order he could best give them.

The fifth session's record shows the intelligence piling up in bricks. Each day added to an edifice no single meeting could have built. For readers, the page marks the debriefing's steady, almost workmanlike pace at the height of its danger.
cia-0000013295:
Viet Cong policy for handling prisoners of every kind is set out in a CIA paper from February 1972. The policy covered Vietnamese military prisoners and political prisoners. It also covered American prisoners held in the south that year. The southern net was broad in its reach. It caught soldiers, officials, and ordinary villagers alike. Each kind was sorted into its own rules, camps, and fates under the system.

The paper surveys that whole net near the war's end. By 1972 the system had run for years and its habits were set. For readers, it is the comprehensive survey: the southern captivity in full, categories and all.
cia-0000013895: A witness saw an American prisoner being taken toward Hanoi, and a CIA note dated October 2, 1967, reports the sighting. Hanoi, the northern capital, held the north's best known prison camps. A man seen on that road was entering the main camp system. Each such report helped officials follow prisoners from capture to confinement.
cia-0000014195: What would follow from a certain U.S. course of action is traced in a CIA paper dated May 5, 1965. The title keeps the chosen act unnamed, yet the paper's task is plain. It worked out the likely chain of effects, near and far. Papers of this kind gave officials a map of results before they signed off on a move.
cia-0000015495: An unidentified object observed in the sky is the whole subject of a CIA record dated in 1958. No place, witness, or shape is named in the title. Records this bare were still worth filing to the watchers of that decade. Each added one line to a vast count, and the count itself became the fact that later readers of the file must reckon with.
cia-0000036295:
A CIA record dated March 2, 1970 has its title deleted, yet its subject still shows through. The surviving line says Latin American terrorists had used kidnapping as a means to their ends. Heavy deletion was common in files on armed groups and their methods.

What remains describes kidnapping as a chosen tactic, used on purpose rather than by chance. Even with its title blacked out, the record adds to the picture of that violent period. It also shows how declassification can leave a file readable in part and hidden in part. The means named in the surviving line is kidnapping used for political ends.
cia-0000041195:
Broadcasts from North Vietnam carried Jane Fonda's alleged impressions of a talk with American prisoners, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1972. The word alleged in the title matters. It marks the account as Hanoi's version, not a proven one. Fonda's visit to the north was then at its height.

Inside, her reported impressions are preserved as the broadcasts gave them out. American monitors weighed each claim against what they knew of the prisons. The file shows the care taken with enemy radio claims. Even a star's reported words were filed as claims to be checked, not as facts to be trusted at first hearing.
cia-0000048995: The assassination of Archbishop Romero fills its own CIA file from 1980, kept with the Truth Commission records. Romero was shot at the altar in March of that year, the murder that announced El Salvador's civil war to the world. The file stands apart from the series' day-to-day cables: the case that overshadowed all the others.
cia-0000049095: ARENA worked on plans in 1984 to amend one of President Duarte's general measures, its title cut off mid-word. A CIA item from that year preserves the plans, kept with the Truth Commission records. The party fought on both tracks at once. Amending a president's program from the right was ARENA's parliamentary road, running beside the armed one.
cia-0000049195: Dissatisfaction spread through El Salvador's officer corps in 1990 over a failure by Chief of Staff Ponce, and a CIA item preserves the mood. Grumbling at the chief of staff, in writing, meant the institution's discipline was fraying near the top. The item survives among the Truth Commission records of the case years.
cia-0000049295: El Salvador's military seized an investigation in 1986, and a CIA item from that year records the takeover, kept with the Truth Commission records. Seizing a case was the surest way to end it: the suspects' own institution became investigator, judge, and archive. The item preserves the moment the file changed hands.
cia-0000049395: Little progress in the Jesuit murder case in El Salvador is reported by declassified CIA document 0000049395, dated February 1, 1991. The item carries a Truth Commission note and stresses slow movement in the case. Readers find a brief dated record whose heading states the stall plainly, useful for following the case through the agency's later files.
cia-0000096495: Progress report on the implementation of Recommendation number two is declassified CIA document 0000096495, dated March 2, 1957. The heading is cut short in the catalog. The brief file is another installment in the numbered recommendation series. It differs from its companions only in the number it tracks. That sameness is a small sign of methodical board follow-up.
cia-0000097995: Memorandum on sightings of Americans in Long Khanh Province and Saigon is declassified CIA document 0000097995, dated November 1, 1976. The heading names two places in Vietnam where Americans were reportedly seen. Readers find a short postwar memorandum record, its subject reported sightings after the war, preserved among the agency's later Vietnam files.
cia-0000124295: A November 1957 CIA item examines batteries made in Britain that may have flown in Sputniks One and Two. The thought that British parts powered Soviet satellites was a claim worth checking at the time. The item preserves the report and the agency's interest in it. Trade questions followed the technical ones: if Western parts had flown, export rules and allied suppliers would both come under hard review in London and Washington.
cia-0000132595: Cuba and Communist China are paired in a CIA document dated August 6, 1960. Two revolutions half a world apart were finding common cause that year. Beijing offered Havana a second communist patron to set against total reliance on Moscow. The short document covers the young relationship between the two states and the visits and talks that built it during 1960.
cia-0000135695: A Spanish document dated 4 January 1961, from the declassified records of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force. Early January found the brigade in training, its landing still a secret plan. The catalog title for this item is the generic series title, with no subject attached. It is preserved in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of a dense run of brigade documents from the first week of 1961.
cia-0000135895: The meeting record dated 2 February 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with the weekly PBSUCCESS meeting with a person whose name is deleted from the heading. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136095: From 6 March 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on continued flights into Toncontin, the airport at Tegucigalpa, kept open by a Lincoln ruling. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136195: A declassified CIA cable dated 2 May 1954 turns to a person, name deleted, being held somewhere the heading cuts off, reported for WELLBANKS. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136395: Briefing guidance for a propaganda asset appears in this 1953 cable. The asset represents, unofficially, a group of Latin American anti-communists who prefer to remain anonymous, and United States interests should be played down. The project's short-range objective was defined as serving PBSUCCESS, with funds allotted in stages as circumstances warrant. Its long-term objective must await the outcome in Guatemala, though the cable argues the work may warrant continuing afterward as a new project.
cia-0000136995: Lessons and themes to push long term fill this June 1954 cable. A new regime must consolidate itself among neighboring states. The themes look past the coup. Guatemala was used by communists, one theme runs. It was used throughout the world. Men who thought they used communists were used instead. The same happens everywhere. Another theme lists communist rule in power. Torture, murder, destruction, and liberty suppressed. It could happen here, the line warns. Complacency let the situation grow, a final theme adds.
cia-0000140395: Research projects for the Artichoke program are listed in this January 1952 document. Each project gets a one-line purpose. Electric shock and hypnotic techniques are to be developed for Artichoke use. Drug techniques are to be developed as well. New interrogation techniques appear on the list. New hypnosis methods based on outside work appear too. Names of researchers and contractors sit in columns lost to poor copying. The page is the mind-control program's early portfolio in outline.
cia-03153695: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/06/06, a CIA publication. The June briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-06775695: THE MONSTER PLOT: COUNTERINTELLIGENCE IN THE CASE OF YURITY IVANOVICH NOSENKO, a CIA document. The defector case. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
cia-06788695: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN, 1961/04/08. The April briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Writers of history may cite it later.
conrad-almayers-folly-1895:
Almayer's Folly, published in 1895, was Joseph Conrad's first novel, written while he was still a merchant seaman. Kaspar Almayer is a Dutch trader on a Borneo river, dreaming of gold and a grand house that will never be finished.

His hopes rest on his daughter Nina, whose love for a Malay prince ruins every plan he has made. Around them, river politics, Arab traders, and colonial greed close in. Conrad already shows his gifts: atmosphere, moral fog, and the slow wreck of a weak man's dream. The great career of Heart of Darkness and Nostromo begins here.
crane-red-badge-1895:
Stephen Crane published The Red Badge of Courage in 1895, at twenty-three, having never seen a battle. He built the novel from veterans' magazines, Tolstoy, and his own imagination. It made him famous in a year, on both sides of the Atlantic.

Henry Fleming, a young Union recruit, dreams of glory and then runs from his first fight, generally identified as Chancellorsville. He longs for a red badge of courage, a wound, to excuse his shame. Chance throws him back into battle, where terror and frenzy carry him to heroism he barely understands. Crane renders war through color, noise, and the private weather of one mind. The novel invented modern war fiction.
eckartshausen-cloud-upon-the-sanctuary-1:
Isabel de Steiger translated Karl von Eckartshausen's Cloud upon the Sanctuary into English for A E Waite's journal The Unknown World in 1895. The German book of 1802 teaches the doctrine of the interior Church. That doctrine holds that a hidden company of the elect guards the heart of faith.

Steiger's version put that teaching before English readers of the Golden Dawn age for the first time. Waite valued the book so highly that he pressed it on the young Aleister Crowley. The six letters speak in a calm, inward tone about prayer, rebirth, and hidden light. In English dress, the work shaped a whole line of later mystic groups.
europmc-pmc10119095:
Gao and co-workers test whether faster biological aging raises the risk of depression and anxiety, in a 2023 study of UK Biobank participants. The study drew on health records from more than four hundred thousand people. Biological age measures how worn the body is, which can differ from age in years.

The team measured biological age and then tracked who later developed depression or anxiety. They found that people aging faster faced higher risk of both conditions. The results suggest that slowing body aging might also protect mental health in later life.
europmc-pmc11098495:
Abdennur and colleagues present a Python toolkit for fine-scale maps of genome folding in this 2024 paper. Hi-C is a method that measures which DNA regions sit near each other inside the cell. Its maps keep growing in size, depth, and detail. Analysis tools had not kept pace, straining storage, memory, and researcher time.

Their suite, cooltools, builds on the cooler file format made for such maps. It offers both a command line tool for computing clusters and a Python interface for interactive work. The design stresses flexible, scalable, and reproducible analysis that users can adapt to new questions. The code is shared openly online. The authors position it for the largest current folding datasets, where older tools stall.
europmc-pmc11102195:
Lin and colleagues review how cancers switch on an immune brake and how that brake is controlled in this 2024 paper. PD-1 is a protein on T cells that, when engaged by its partner PD-L1, damps T cell attack. That damping keeps immunity in balance in health. Cancer cells exploit the same axis to escape immune attack.

Antibodies that block the pair restore T cell activity and have won notable success in cancer therapy, the authors note. The review gathers all the controls on the pair's levels and activity in cancer. These span gene changes, signal paths, and RNA-level tuning. It also covers the pair's roles in diseases where the immune system attacks the body. The authors argue that knowing the controls points to ways to make blockade work for more patients.
europmc-pmc11126395:
GBD 2021 Demographics Collaborators rebuild population counts for 204 countries from 1950 to 2021 in this 2024 study. Sound counts of deaths, life expectancy, and population size are crucial for judging health trends. The COVID-19 pandemic made timely estimates urgent. This round gives special weight to how deaths and life expectancy shifted during 2020 and 2021.

The team used 22,223 data sources for mortality and 2,026 for population counts, they report. Extra sources captured migration, the HIV epidemic, and shocks from wars, famines, and disasters. A smoothing statistical model filled gaps across place and time. Excess deaths due to the pandemic were estimated from a dedicated subset of sources. Results include 811 subnational locations. The authors present the dataset as the demographic base for the wider burden study.
europmc-pmc12280795:
Porsteinsson and colleagues described early Alzheimer diagnosis practice in 2021. The disease moves along a long path before dementia. It starts silently, then brings mild memory or behavior change. Clinicians are urged to spot it at those early stages.

Early and accurate diagnosis helps patients plan and act sooner. Lifestyle steps may preserve quality of life longer. Real clinics face barriers like short visits and hard tests. Symptoms also get dismissed as normal aging too often. Porsteinsson reviews tools and habits that help. Better detection sets up better care and screening.
europmc-pmc1247195:
Richardson, Thomson, Best, and Elliott tested disease-mapping models by simulation in 2004. Small-area health data are sparse, so models smooth risk estimates. Bayesian models, which blend data with prior structure, do most smoothing. Doubts persisted about how much truth smoothing erases.

Simulations showed the models lean conservative overall. They rarely flagged false high-risk areas, even with sparse data. But they missed areas with under twofold excess risk. Misses were worst when expected counts fell below 50. Mixture models smoothed less when data were richer. Richardson maps when smoothed maps can be trusted.
europmc-pmc1484495:
Viruses that infect ocean bacteria often carry stolen sunlight genes. Sullivan and co-authors surveyed that theft in 2006. They screened 33 cultured cyanophages, viruses of marine cyanobacteria, plus viral DNA from sea samples. They hunted two core genes of photosystem II, the cell's light-harvesting engine.

Of the phage genomes, 88 percent held one gene, psbA, and half held both genes. All myoviruses carried psbA, while some smaller virus groups lacked it. Tree analysis suggests whole genes passed from host to phage in a few discrete events: four for psbA, two for psbD. Sullivan links gene carriage to how long an infection lies latent.
europmc-pmc1551995:
Arsenic in drinking water scars lungs decades after exposure. Smith and co-authors studied the Chilean city of Antofagasta in 2006. Its water ran very high in arsenic from 1958 to 1971, then a cleanup plant was built. They compared death rates there with the rest of Chile.

Adults aged 30 to 49 who were exposed as small children died of lung cancer at seven times the expected rate. Deaths from bronchiectasis, a widening of the airways, ran twelve times higher. For those exposed in the womb, bronchiectasis deaths ran 46 times higher. Smith concludes early arsenic exposure leaves lifelong lung damage.
europmc-pmc1586195:
Patients' own ratings of their health are now key trial endpoints. Revicki and co-authors set out in 2006 how to judge whether such rating tools respond to change, and how big a change matters. US drug guidance had raised fresh questions on these points.

They recommend estimating the minimal important difference from several anchor-based methods. Those tie score changes to clinical or patient-judged benchmarks. Distribution-based figures, like effect size, serve as backup. The estimates are then triangulated into one value or a narrow range. Revicki warns the right value varies by population, and confidence in it grows with use.
europmc-pmc1810395:
Sittka, Vogel and co-authors showed in 2007 that a small RNA-binding protein is essential for Salmonella to cause disease. The protein, Hfq, helps small regulatory RNAs pair with their target messages. Salmonella typhimurium lives inside host cells and causes gut and whole-body infection.

Deleting the hfq gene left the bacteria highly weakened in mice after both oral and gut-bypassing infection. The mutant invaded surface cells poorly and grew badly inside both those cells and macrophages, the immune cells that should kill it. Surprisingly, most defects did not stem from loss of the stress factor RpoS, Hfq's best-known target. Instead, Hfq controlled movement, surface protein levels, and invasion through a web of small RNAs. The mutation also kept the membrane stress response switched on.
europmc-pmc1828695:
Zipfel and colleagues reported in 2007 that losing two immune-control genes raises the risk of a rare kidney disease. Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome damages red blood cells and kidneys, and it is tied to faulty control of the complement system, an immune attack cascade. Known mutations hit several complement regulators.

In two separate patient groups, deletion of the related genes CFHR1 and CFHR3 was tied to the disease. Three patients carried a deletion of about 84 thousand DNA letters that removed both genes but left the main factor H gene intact. Matching repeat sequences flank the genes, and faulty recombination between those repeats likely causes the loss. Blood from patients lacking the pair protected red cells poorly against complement attack, giving the genes a clear regulatory role.
europmc-pmc1892795:
Winstanley, Eagle and Robbins reviewed in 2006 how impulsivity is modeled in animals to shed light on ADHD. Impulsivity, acting without foresight, appears in ADHD, mania, and substance abuse. The term covers several distinct behaviors that may have distinct brain bases, so each needs its own test.

The review breaks impulsivity into parts and matches each to a rodent task borrowed from human testing. Three paradigms get the closest look. First is the five-choice serial reaction time task. Second is the stop-signal task, which tests halting a response already launched. Third, delay-discounting tasks measure impatience for rewards. The authors weigh what animal work with these tasks has taught about the brain circuits and chemistry of impulsivity. They also judge how well each model translates back to the clinic and to ADHD treatment.
europmc-pmc1933595:
Bruno and Selig assembled in 2007 the first region-wide account of coral loss across the Indo-Pacific, home to 75 percent of the world's reefs. Heat waves and other pressures had caused mass coral deaths, but the timing, pace, and patchiness of the loss were largely unmeasured in that ocean basin.

Their database pooled 6,001 quantitative surveys of 2,667 reefs from 1968 to 2004. By 2003, coral cover averaged only 22.1 percent, and just seven of 390 reefs surveyed that year topped 60 percent cover. Yearly loss ran near one percent over two decades, and about two percent a year from 1997 to 2003. Reefs re-surveyed across years lost 0.72 percent a year. Cover was oddly uniform between subregions, and decline began decades earlier than assumed, even on well-managed reefs.
europmc-pmc2020495:
von Elm and co-authors, with the STROBE Initiative, published reporting guidelines in 2007 for observational studies. Much medical research observes people rather than assigning treatments. Poor reporting makes it hard to judge a study's strengths, weaknesses and wider relevance. The group aimed to define what a complete and accurate report should contain. They covered cohort, case-control and cross-sectional designs.

A two-day workshop in September 2004 brought together method experts, researchers and journal editors. Drafting and repeated revision produced a checklist of 22 items. Eighteen items apply to all three designs, and four are design-specific. The items span a paper's title and abstract, its introduction and methods, and its results and discussion sections. A separate explanation document gives the reasoning for each item.
europmc-pmc2065895:
Beerenwinkel and colleagues built a maths model in 2007 for how colorectal cancer develops over time. Cancer grows through a series of genetic changes that free cells from normal cooperation. Recent genome studies found about 100 mutations in single colorectal tumours. As many as 20 may drive the disease. The team used published sequencing data from Sjöblom and others to model that process.

Their model uses the Wright-Fisher process, a standard model of random genetic change in populations. It yields a formula for the expected waiting time until cancer appears. Selection mattered more than population size or mutation rate. The observed diversity fits a normal mutation rate if each driver mutation gives about a 1 percent growth advantage. Many small steps, not a few big ones, can explain progression.
europmc-pmc2092395:
von Ahlfen, Missel, Bendrat and Schlumpberger tested in 2007 what determines RNA quality in archived tissue samples. Hospitals store vast numbers of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded specimens, called FFPE samples. They could power gene studies, but fixation and storage damage RNA. Evidence on which handling steps matter most was mostly anecdotal. The team varied storage, fixation time and specimen size systematically in rat tissues.

Freshly embedded samples gave surprisingly intact RNA, with integrity scores around seven or higher. Storage temperature had a profound effect on RNA fragmentation over twelve months. Samples kept at 4 degrees stayed visibly better preserved than warmer-stored ones. RNA taken within one to three days of embedding was the least fragmented. The results matter for any method starting with copying RNA into DNA, such as RT-PCR or microarrays.
europmc-pmc2117995: A medical paper contributing a differential stain for connective tissue. The microscope slide, colored. This article preserves that staining method. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128195: A medical paper on experimental syphilis in the rabbit, bone and cartilage affections. The rabbit bones. This article preserves that venereology. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
europmc-pmc2128695: A medical paper with studies on the d'Herelle phenomenon with Bacillus dysenteriae. The bacteriophage. This article preserves that virology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131095: A medical paper on the surface composition of normal and sensitized mammalian blood cells. The cells' skin. This article preserves that hematology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140395: A biology paper on ionic radius and ionic efficiency. The ions' size. This article preserves that chemistry. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2140495: A biology paper with studies on bioluminescence, the specificity of luciferin and luciferase. The glowing chemistry. This article preserves that biochemistry. It waits for future eyes. The historical record keeps it. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2140595: A biology paper with studies in protoplasm poisoning, phenols. The poisoned protoplasm. This article preserves that toxicology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2225395:
Varkonyi-Gasic, Wu, Wood, Walton and Hellens published a protocol in 2007 for detecting microRNAs with extreme sensitivity. MicroRNAs are tiny non-coding RNAs central to development and stress responses in plants and animals. Gel-based detection methods are slow, insensitive and low-throughput. Their looped RT-PCR method first copies the microRNA into DNA, then amplifies it for measurement, in both end-point and real-time versions.

The method detected microRNAs from as little as 20 picograms of total RNA from plant tissue. It also worked with RNA from just 0.1 microlitres of phloem sap, the fluid in plant transport tissue. A variant assay improved specificity for scarce microRNAs. Those are hard to measure reliably at low levels in small samples of plant material. Using it, the team showed microRNAs are expressed differently in phloem sap than in surrounding vascular tissue.
europmc-pmc2361795:
Huxley and co-authors pooled 36 studies on type 2 diabetes and pancreatic cancer in 2005. Pancreatic cancer kills about 227,000 people a year worldwide, yet few causes are known besides smoking. Diabetes often appears alongside it, but the cancer itself can trigger diabetes, so cause and effect are tangled.

Their combined odds ratio was 1.82, meaning people with diabetes had roughly 80% higher odds of pancreatic cancer. Risk was highest soon after diabetes appeared. People diagnosed under four years earlier had an odds ratio of 2.1, versus 1.5 for those with diabetes for five years or more. That pattern suggests some new diabetes is an early sign of hidden cancer. Still, the authors judged the results support a modest true effect of diabetes itself.
europmc-pmc2364095:
O'Byrne and Dalgleish argued in 2001 that long-lasting inflammation can itself cause cancer. Some cancers follow chronic infections, but other long-term inflamed tissues also turn cancerous with no infection found. That pattern, they proposed, means the inflamed setting itself gives cancer what it needs to start.

They described how inflamed tissue raises an enzyme called COX-2, which drives messengers that can mute immune attack and spur new blood vessels. The same setting can speed cell division and block the normal self-destruct program for damaged cells. Inflamed cells also produce reactive oxygen chemicals that can damage DNA and cause mutations. The authors suggested that calming inflammation, cutting vessel growth, and boosting cell-based immunity could prevent many common cancers, a strategy they urged researchers to test.
europmc-pmc2515195:
Sittka and co-authors mapped the RNA targets of a bacterial control protein in Salmonella in this 2008 study. The protein, Hfq, binds short RNA molecules and helps them switch genes on or off after the genes are read. Which RNAs it touches, and what that means for the cell, was only partly known.

By sequencing 350,000 RNA fragments pulled down with tagged Hfq, the team found 727 bound messenger RNAs. The search more than doubled the known small RNAs in Salmonella, bringing the total to 64, and about half of them bind Hfq. Hfq proved to influence nearly a fifth of all Salmonella genes. These include whole sets for invading host cells. They also include sets for building flagella, the whipping tails bacteria swim with.
europmc-pmc2571995:
Keating and a large team of collaborators described in 2008 a purpose-built gene chip for cardiovascular research. Genome-wide scans had uncovered many DNA variants linked to heart and metabolic disease, but each variant's effect is small, so confirming them demands huge pooled studies. The team designed a gene-centric array holding about 50,000 SNPs, the single-letter variants used as markers.

The chip covers roughly 2,000 priority genes tied to cardiovascular, metabolic, and inflammatory conditions, tagged to capture diversity across the major HapMap populations. High-priority genes get denser coverage than genome-wide tools provide, especially for African samples. The group planned to genotype DNA from over 200,000 well-characterised people and release much of the data publicly. Shared results would support replication checks, rare variant hunts, and combined analyses across cohorts.
europmc-pmc2694995:
Schiffman, Clifford, and Buonaguro described in 2009 how an expert panel judged which human papillomavirus types count as cancer-causing, focusing on the hardest, weakest cases. Nearly all cervical cancer traces to persistent infection with one of a small set of these viruses, out of more than 100 types. Types 16 and 18 are proven heavyweights. The borderline types are where science strains.

The judgments matter in practice: screening tests and vaccines are built around the list of guilty types. Yet at the weak end, studies strain against confounding and misclassification, since infections cluster and tests err. The authors lay out the approach taken by a World Health Organization working group for the official re-assessment, showing its reasoning openly for debate. Calling a weak type carcinogenic, or clearing it, they argue, should be done with stated rules, not impressions.
europmc-pmc2716295:
Helfrich and co-authors built in 2009 the ORCA survey, a tool to judge whether a health organization is ready to adopt proven care practices. It follows the PARIHS framework, which says success rests on evidence, context, and facilitation, meaning skilled help to make change happen. That framework had guides but no tested measure to score its parts.

They tested a seventy-seven-item survey from three Veterans Health projects, grouped into nineteen subscales under the three main scales. Facilitation and context scales held together well, while the evidence scale fell below the usual reliability bar and lost three items. Two subscales also failed to load as the framework predicts, so more testing is still needed.
europmc-pmc2716495:
Lowery and co-authors searched in 2009 for microRNA signatures that predict receptor status in breast cancer. Tumors are classed by whether they carry estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors, which guide treatment, and those traits can shift as disease advances. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that are often faulty in cancer.

Profiling hundreds of microRNAs in twenty-nine early tumors and training neural networks, a form of pattern-learning software, yielded distinct signatures for each receptor. Checks in ninety-five more tumors showed one marker, miR-342, was highest in luminal B tumors and lowest in triple-negative tumors, the hardest type to treat. Another marker rose in tumors lacking estrogen and progesterone receptors.
europmc-pmc2757795:
McVean gave in 2009 a genealogical interpretation of principal components analysis, a statistical method widely used to reveal structure in genetic variation across places and ethnic groups. The method projects each sample onto main axes, but what those projections mean in terms of migration, isolation, and admixture was poorly understood. Practitioners often read history into the plots without a formal basis.

He shows that for SNP data, a sample's projection can be derived directly from average coalescent times, the times back to common ancestors, between pairs of genomes. That links the plot to Wright's Fst, a classic measure of population split. SNP ascertainment, how variants were chosen, distorts the projection in a largely simple and predictable way, which sharpens empirical inference.
europmc-pmc2800195:
Melzer and co-authors checked in 2010 whether bisphenol A in urine tracks with heart disease in United States adults. BPA is used heavily in food and drink packaging, and an earlier survey round had linked it to heart disease and diabetes. The team analyzed two rounds of the national NHANES survey, covering about fifteen hundred adults each.

Urine BPA levels were lower in the later round than in the earlier one. Even so, higher BPA tracked with more reported coronary heart disease in the later round and in both rounds combined. The diabetes link reached clear levels only in the combined data. Liver enzyme links were weak and mixed, and the authors call for work on how BPA might act.
europmc-pmc2821895:
Moher, Schulz, Simera, and Altman wrote guidance in 2010 for people who build reporting guidelines for health research. Reporting guidelines are checklists that tell authors what a study write-up must include. Poor reporting is common: one check found treatment details too thin to copy in about half of published articles, which wastes research money and blocks fair judgment of results.

Coming from the EQUATOR network, which works to improve how health research is published, the guidance lays out recommended steps for developing a guideline properly. A review of eighty-one existing guidelines had shown many were built weakly. The authors stress an explicit method and a consensus process, so new checklists rest on agreement rather than one group's habits.
europmc-pmc2857295:
Guang-Zhi Tong and co-authors reported in a 2007 letter on a new, far deadlier form of pig disease then sweeping China. The illness was highly pathogenic porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, a viral disease of swine herds. Fever stayed high, ears turned blue, and pigs of all ages died in large numbers.

Testing farm samples from many provinces, Tong found the syndrome virus in almost every case, with most samples positive and other pig viruses absent. One isolate, named HuN4, carried two deletions in a viral gene called Nsp2, plus wide changes elsewhere. Piglets given the virus all died within three weeks, and a wider survey found the same deleted strain across twelve provinces.
europmc-pmc2948795:
Fox and Rosen reviewed how well HIV treatment programmes in sub-Saharan Africa kept patients on therapy, in a 2010 systematic review covering 2007 to 2009 reports. Staying on antiretroviral drugs for years is essential, yet clinics lose many patients.

Across dozens of cohorts totalling well over two hundred thousand starters, pooled retention fell steadily, from the mid-eighties percent at six months to the low seventies at three years. Leaving follow-up caused more losses than death. Most patients were women starting treatment in their late thirties with low immune cell counts, underlining the scale of support needed.
europmc-pmc2987895:
Laureys led a European task force proposing a new name, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, for the condition long called the vegetative state, in a 2010 article. Such patients open their eyes after coma yet show only reflex movements and no response to commands.

Many clinicians dislike the old label, which to the public hints at being vegetable-like and has drawn pressure from rights campaigns. Brain imaging studies also warn that some seemingly unaware patients may retain hidden awareness, and diagnosis is sometimes wrong. A neutral name, the group argues, respects patients while the science of awareness catches up.
europmc-pmc3042595:
Ehring and colleagues validated in 2011 a questionnaire that measures repetitive negative thinking without tying it to any single disorder. Worry and rumination, the looping over bad thoughts, appear across depression, anxiety, and many other conditions, yet older scales asked about one disorder's content only. Their fifteen item scale instead asks about the process itself, such as how intrusive and hard to stop the thoughts feel.

Two studies with over eighteen hundred people, including patients, supported the design. One broad factor covered the whole scale, with three smaller factors for core features, felt uselessness, and mental drain. Scores were stable over time and lined up with older worry and rumination scales and with depression and anxiety symptoms. The authors offer the scale as a tool for studying one shared process behind many disorders.
europmc-pmc3048395:
van Passel and colleagues sequenced in 2011 the genome of a gut bacterium that lives by eating the mucus lining of the human intestine. The bacterium, Akkermansia muciniphila, had only recently been isolated and belongs to a deep branching bacterial group. It sits in the protective mucus layer and uses mucus as both food and nitrogen source.

Its genome holds many candidate genes for mucus cutting enzymes, though oddly none for the usual mucus gripping parts. Virus traces scattered through the genome show that phages shaped its evolution. Mining dozens of gut DNA surveys found its relatives in many people, sometimes as several strains in one gut, and at widely varying abundance. At least eight species seem to exist in the genus. The genome turns an abundant but mysterious gut resident into a workable study subject.
europmc-pmc3068995:
de Vries and colleagues showed in 2011 that influenza A virus has a second way into cells besides its textbook route. The known route uses a protein cage and a pinch off motor to pull the virus inside. Blocking that motor stopped entry completely in plain salt solution, but adding blood serum opened another door that the blocker could not close.

A drug that blocks a bulk drinking process of cells shut the side door, and only the two drugs together stopped entry fully in serum. Virus particles were seen sharing the same internal bubbles as a tracer for that drinking process. Mutations and inhibitors of growth signal pathways also hit the side route. The authors conclude the virus rides a process called macropinocytosis when conditions allow. That flexibility may help explain how flu infects varied cell types.
europmc-pmc3098195:
McPherson and coauthors built in 2011 an algorithm, deFuse, to find gene fusions in the RNA sequences of tumors. Fusions, where two genes are stitched into one by chromosome rearrangements, drive some lymphomas and sarcomas and can be drug targets. RNA sequencing can reveal them, but early search methods missed many by demanding perfect matches and assuming breaks land only at known gene joints.

Their method considers every alignment and every possible break point, then filters candidates with a trained classifier built on confirmed true and false fusions. That raised detection sensitivity clearly over earlier tools. Running it on ovarian tumors, an ovarian cell line, and sarcomas, they reported the first fusions ever found in ovarian cancer. Several fusions changed how strongly their partner genes were expressed. The authors argue fusions are common in this cancer and belong in its molecular profile.
europmc-pmc3111195:
Pamela Munster and colleagues reported a 2011 cancer trial in the British Journal of Cancer for women whose breast cancer had stopped responding to hormone treatment. The trial paired a daily hormone pill with a second drug that loosens chemical tags on proteins, an approach lab work suggested could restore hormone response. Just over forty women with spreading disease took part.

About one woman in five saw her tumour shrink, and two in five gained shrinkage or lasting stability, with responses lasting around ten months on average. Blood tests showed that stronger tag changes and higher starting levels of one target protein tracked with benefit. The pairing was tolerated well and supports further testing with blood markers to pick likely responders.
europmc-pmc3139595:
Jin-Hui Wang and colleagues tested whether brain network maps give the same answer twice in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Researchers increasingly chart the resting brain as a network of linked regions and summarise it with graph measures. The team rescanned volunteers within an hour and again after months, then checked how steady twelve global and six local measures stayed.

Global measures proved shaky overall, shifting with time gap, sign handling, and how links were weighted. Local measures varied widely by region and type, though connection count per region was the steadiest of all. Hub regions in higher brain areas showed fair steadiness. Computer simulations blamed sensitivity to noise in the link data. The paper guides analysts toward the schemes and measures that can be trusted.
europmc-pmc3153395:
Joseph Verbalis and colleagues linked long-term low blood sodium to bone loss in a 2010 paper in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. Low sodium is common in older people and was already tied to unsteady walking and falls. A fall only breaks bones more easily if the bones themselves are weakened, so the team tested both rats and national survey data.

Rats kept low in sodium for three months lost about a third of measured bone density, through faster bone breakdown and slower building. In the human survey, even mild low sodium came with notably higher odds of osteoporosis at the hip. The authors urge bone checks for patients with chronic low sodium, a risk factor hiding in plain sight.
europmc-pmc3189095:
Taek Soon Lee and colleagues built a standardised plasmid library for engineering bacteria in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Biological Engineering. Complex engineered systems often need several plasmids and switches in one cell, yet nobody had measured how the parts behave in combination. The team constructed nearly a hundred compatible plasmids mixing replication origins, resistance markers, and inducible promoters under one assembly standard.

Each plasmid was measured across inducer doses, in the presence of other inducers, and in several growth media, with results published as standard datasheets. A three-plasmid test showed how sharing a cell shifts copy numbers. With numbers in hand, users can assemble multi-plasmid systems and predict expression far better than by trial and error.
europmc-pmc3219295:
Nele Brusselaers and colleagues reviewed severe burn injury across Europe in this 2010 systematic review in Critical Care. They searched the literature from 1985 to 2009 for studies of hospitalized patients with severe burns. They gathered data on how often such injuries happen and what causes them. They also recorded how often patients die.

Seventy-six studies covering more than one hundred eighty-six thousand patients qualified. Annual incidence varied widely between countries but trended downward over time, and nearly half of patients were children under sixteen. Flames, scalds, and contact burns were the leading causes, with scalds dominating in children. Death rates fell over time; older age, larger burned area, and chronic disease raised the risk. Organ failure and sepsis were the commonest causes of death. The authors call for European registration systems.
europmc-pmc3224595:
Cristian Lasagna-Reeves and colleagues tested which form of the tau protein harms the brain, in this 2011 study in Molecular Neurodegeneration. In Alzheimer's disease, tau clumps into tangles, but whether the tangles themselves are the toxic species was disputed. Small clusters called oligomers, formed before fibers appear, were emerging as the prime suspect.

The team injected laboratory-made human tau into the brains of normal mice. Oligomers impaired the animals' memory consolidation, while tau fibers and single tau molecules did not. Oligomers also cut levels of proteins needed at synapses, weakened a key part of the mitochondria's energy machinery, and switched on a cell-death enzyme. The authors identify oligomers as an acutely toxic species and a target for protective treatments.
europmc-pmc3224695:
Elaine Barnett-Page and James Thomas critically reviewed methods for synthesizing qualitative research in this 2009 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Ways of combining findings across interview and observational studies had multiplied, especially in health research. Funders and researchers needed a map to tell the methods apart and choose among them.

The authors trace the links between methods and the contrasts between them. Much of the difference comes down to philosophy of knowledge. Methods split broadly into realist and idealist camps. That split explains their different stances on judging study quality. It also explains how much reinterpretation each allows. The review advises commissioners to start from the kind of product they want, then pick the method, or family of methods, that fits.
europmc-pmc3261895:
Thomas Derrien and colleagues presented a fast way to compute the mappability of a genome, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Mappability asks, for each stretch of a reference genome, whether sequencing reads can be placed there uniquely. Without it, results from massive parallel sequencing are easy to misread, because reads landing in repetitive regions cannot be trusted to one address.

Their mapping-based algorithm computes mappability up to a chosen number of mismatches far faster than earlier approaches. The team explored how mappability looks across whole genomes and within gene families in several organisms, releasing visual tracks for browsing. Mappability varied greatly between species and gene classes. They show practical uses in calling variants, measuring gene expression, and designing paired-end experiments, arguing the concept deserves a routine place in analysis.
europmc-pmc3277595:
Chengwei Luo and colleagues ran a head-to-head comparison of the two dominant sequencing platforms on the same microbial community, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Metagenomic studies rely on these machines, but whether Roche 454 and Illumina platforms recover the same diversity, with equally trustworthy assemblies, was unclear. The team sequenced one DNA sample from a freshwater plankton community on both.

Despite very different read lengths and protocols, the two platforms painted a comparable picture. Their assemblies overlapped across most of their sequence. The estimated abundances of genes and genotypes also agreed closely. Judged by base-call errors, frameshifts, and contig lengths, Illumina matched or beat 454. Checks against eighteen sequenced isolate genomes confirmed the pattern. The authors offer quantitative error estimates by sample complexity and composition, as a practical guide for designing future studies.
europmc-pmc3292895:
McDonald, Winum, Supuran, and Dedhar reviewed efforts to attack tumors through an oxygen starvation protein in 2012. When solid tumors outgrow their blood supply, low oxygen switches on a protein called carbonic anhydrase IX in many cancer cells. That protein helps cells keep their inner acidity in a range that suits growth, while the space around them turns more acidic and easier to invade.

Blocking the protein with antibodies or small drugs slowed tumor growth and spread in lab studies, the authors report. Several such agents were moving through early testing when the review was written. The team presents this approach as a targeted treatment strategy that exploits a weakness tumors create for themselves.
europmc-pmc3320095:
Lamark and Johansen reviewed how cells dispose of clumped proteins through a targeted cleanup route, in a 2012 article. Proteins constantly stick together inside cells. Some clumps serve useful purposes, while others form when stress or errors damage proteins beyond repair. Small clumps can be dissolved and fed to the cell's shredding machines, but solid aggregates are too large for that route.

Whole aggregates instead get swallowed by the cell's bulk recycling system, a process the authors call aggrephagy. Special receptor proteins recognize the clumps, move them, and load them into the parcels that deliver cargo for destruction. The review traces each step, from clump formation to final disposal. It also examines diseases where clumps build up, including brain disorders, to show what happens when this cleanup fails.
europmc-pmc3321295:
Tikellis and Thomas reviewed a blood pressure control enzyme that acts as a counterweight in its hormone system, in a 2012 article. The enzyme, ACE2, resembles the well known target of many blood pressure drugs but is not blocked by them. Its main job is breaking down a vessel tightening hormone and producing a smaller fragment that does roughly the opposite.

Mice lacking the enzyme carry about double the usual level of the tightening hormone, while the calming fragment nearly vanishes. The enzyme's activity rises when hormone levels climb, forming a natural brake. Its levels fall in high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart and vessel disease. The authors survey strategies to boost it, from gene delivery to lab made enzyme, as ways to protect organs in those conditions.
europmc-pmc3321795:
Foy and colleagues reported a case suggesting Zika virus passed between people without a mosquito bite, in a 2011 paper. Zika is a mosquito carried virus related to dengue and yellow fever. Two American scientists fell ill with it after fieldwork in Senegal in 2008, where they had been studying mosquitoes.

Blood tests confirmed Zika infection in both scientists. After one of them returned home to Colorado, his wife also developed the infection, although she had not traveled and local mosquitoes were an unlikely route. The timing and evidence point to direct contact between the couple, most likely sexual transmission. The authors present the case as the first suggestion that this virus can spread person to person, a possibility that matters for how infections in returning travelers are handled.
europmc-pmc3322595:
Afonine and colleagues described a widely used program for polishing atomic models of proteins against X ray data, in a 2012 paper. In crystallography, researchers bounce X rays off protein crystals and then refine a model until it matches the measured pattern. The program, phenix.refine, is part of the PHENIX software suite built for exactly that task.

The program handles data across a wide range of sharpness and offers many ways to describe a model, from rigid chunks to flexible individual atoms. The paper walks through its major features rather than presenting new experiments, pointing readers to detailed references for each method. The authors' stated aim is progress toward refinement that runs itself, needing less expert hand tuning. The tool has become a standard step between raw diffraction data and a published structure.
europmc-pmc3356395:
Schulz and a large team at a stem cell company described how to manufacture pancreatic progenitor cells from human embryonic stem cells at clinical scale. A diabetes cell therapy needs vast, consistent batches, so they built the whole pipeline, from frozen cell banks to final differentiation, under manufacturing-grade conditions.

Starting from qualified banks of the CyT49 cell line, they expanded cells, then clustered them in rotating suspension culture and applied a four-stage, two-week differentiation protocol. The resulting populations were reproducibly rich in pancreatic lineages, and after implantation into mice they matured into insulin-secreting tissue that protected against chemically induced diabetes. The process is offered as ready for clinical entry.
europmc-pmc3398395:
Price synthesized twenty years of brain imaging of language in 2012, covering heard speech, speaking, and reading. Hundreds of PET and scanner studies had accumulated since the field began. Price grouped their conclusions by type of processing and followed the order they appeared.

Many findings replicated so often that some conclusions are now beyond dispute. The review folds them into an anatomical model naming the main language areas and their most consistent jobs. Some processes sit in one structure, like raw hearing, while others, like sound patterning of speech, arise from networks joining hearing, movement, and meaning. The hardest open problem, Price says, is how regions work together.
europmc-pmc3465795:
Cruts, Theuns, and Van Broeckhoven described shared mutation databases for brain diseases in Human Mutation in 2012. The databases collect gene changes behind inherited forms of Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia, and Parkinson disease. Each entry is curated by experts and linked to clinical, genetic, and lab details, so doctors and researchers can check a single mutation quickly.

Pooling all entries let the authors spot broad patterns. Most mutations turned up in just one family, while a handful of common ones accounted for a large share of families in each disease. Most genes in the databases were tied to more than one diagnosis. Cruts's team argues that only pooled, curated records can reveal such patterns.
europmc-pmc3469495:
Bolognesi and a large team traced how double-stranded RNA kills western corn rootworm larvae, in a 2012 PLoS ONE paper. The rootworm is a major corn pest, and feeding it RNA that silences one of its own genes can kill it. The team targeted a gene called Snf7, which the larva needs for moving materials inside its cells.

They found the RNA must be fairly long to work; short pieces failed because gut cells did not take them up. After feeding, the target message fell first, then its protein, and silencing spread beyond the gut within a day. Growth stalled and the larvae died. Bolognesi's account lays out each step, guiding design of RNA-based pest control.

french-constitution-1795:
The National Convention adopted the Constitution of the Year Three in 1795, as the French Revolution cooled into reaction. The Terror had ended with Robespierre's fall, and the Thermidorean rulers sought order above all. Their charter built a government designed to block both kings and mobs.

It created the Directory: five directors holding executive power, checked by two councils of elected deputies. Voting rights were again tied to property, shutting out the poor men the 1793 charter had embraced. A declaration of duties stood beside the rights of man, stressing obedience and order. The charter of the Revolution's weary middle age fenced liberty about with caution. The Directory it founded lasted four years before Napoleon's coup swept it away.
frus-1861-d195:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Cassius M. Clay on 21 May 1861. The letter is document 195 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's May orders to Clay match the stern line sent to London that same day. Russia needed less warning than Britain, but the form was kept. The letter shows the Secretary holding even friendly courts to the same clear terms. Friendly courts still had to be told the terms, lest warmth be mistaken for license. Terms kept clear kept warmth from cooling, as the Russian file went on to prove.

Orders from Washington reached Mr. Harvey in a State Department letter dated 21 August 1861. It stands as Document 295 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d95:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 October 1861. The letter is document 95 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Lyons spoke for a government that held the Union's fate in its hands. His letters to Seward were polite in form and firm in point. This one brings the British view into the record in its own words, not filtered through an American envoy. Lyons's cool style hid a sharp eye for the weak points of the Union cause. A sharp eye behind a cool style made Lyons a match for any chief he faced.
frus-1862-d195:
A second Seward note to Lord Lyons bears the date 3 December 1861 and stands as Document 195 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons represented Britain in Washington; Seward spoke for the Lincoln government as Secretary of State.

Two notes in one day suggest business split by topic, a common practice when talks were tense. The month was dominated by the Trent affair, the seizure of Confederate envoys from a British ship, which had London sending troops to Canada. Every Seward-Lyons note of this date sat under that shadow, whatever its errand. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d295:
Dated 15 July 1862, Document 295 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-July found Lincoln privately drafting an emancipation order and Congress passing sterner war laws. None of that was public when Seward wrote. His letter to Paris belongs to the surface calm of the file in a month when the war's deepest change was being prepared in secret. A contrast the printed record preserves well. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d395:
Bayard Taylor, the travel writer who served as secretary of the American legation in St. Petersburg, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 October 1862. It survives as Document 395 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the record printed with the President's annual message.

Russia was one of the few great powers that stayed warm toward the Union during the Civil War. Reports from St. Petersburg told Washington how the tsar's court read the war and the fight over slavery. Read with the rest of the Russian file, the letter shows why Lincoln's government prized that friendship so highly.
frus-1862-d495:
On 16 April 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 495 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record of American diplomacy.

Mid-April brought the Union a run of successes. The capture of New Orleans crowned them soon after. Pike's reports relayed how the Dutch received the improving story. The Netherlands had no cause to love the Confederacy, but its merchants wanted the seas safe and the war short. A minister's letter in such weeks did double duty: it reported opinion and it reported the small formal business of the post. The dispatch keeps the Dutch file's steady weekly rhythm.
frus-1862-d595:
Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 July 1862, though it is printed after Seward's instruction of 14 July. It is Document 595 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The interleaving of the Mexican file is the Atlantic and overland post at work. Report and answer crossed in transit. The printers followed the office file rather than the calendar. Corwin's July letter described the French campaign's progress and the republic's straits in the summer heat. For Washington, such reports kept the Mexican question alive on paper through a season when American attention was consumed by Virginia. The document is best read in date order with its neighbors, as one voice in a slow, grave conversation.
frus-1862-d695: On 6 May 1862, a Mr. Crosby wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 695 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. The evidence names the writer and the date, but it does not state the post Crosby held or the place he wrote from. This note stays at that level.
frus-1862-d95:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 9 July 1862. It stands as Document 95 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d195:
From his London post on 8 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 195 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d295:
From Washington on 19 September 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 295 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d395: On 19 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 395 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d495:
A letter of 7 May 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 495 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note.
frus-1863p1-d595:
Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons received a letter dated 23 July 1863 from Secretary William H. Seward. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d695:
Dated 25 November 1863, this dispatch went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 695 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, the last note in this short run of the series.

Seward's late November mail came as the year turned toward winter and a new year of war. Keeping Britain neutral stayed at the top of his list. Each note to Lyons, this one among them, served that aim in a small, direct way. The reader closes this run with a sense of the whole. Peace with Britain was kept not by one grand act, but by steady paper work.
frus-1863p1-d95:
Charles Francis Adams sent this third dispatch of 26 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 95 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By the close of February the London file had grown into a near-daily record. Adams's reports charted a Britain that stayed, on the whole, at arm's length from the war, while the South's friends pushed for more. This letter ends his three-sheet day. It is the kind of steady, exact work that made his legation the model of wartime service, and the volume the record of it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d195:
Lieutenant General Joseph Stilwell, chief of staff to China's Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, drafted a set of proposals in November 1943 for the coming conference at Cairo. Written at Chungking, the paper sets out what Chiang's government wanted from its allies for the war against Japan.

The core plan is to build ninety Chinese combat divisions in three groups of thirty, plus one or two armored divisions, trained and equipped in stages through January 1945. China would join in retaking Burma from Ledo and Yunnan. In return, Chiang expects American arms for all ninety divisions, a strong Fourteenth Air Force, a larger Chinese air force. Later he expects American divisions to help seize the Canton and Hong Kong area.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d295: Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a one-line telegram from Washington on 23 November 1943 carrying news from Marshal Stalin. Stalin, who was at the front, states that he will arrive not later than the 28th or 29th at the appointed place, meaning Tehran. The word had reached Washington in a note of 22 November from Molotov to Hamilton, forwarded the same day in a telegram signed by Ambassador Harriman.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d395:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent President Roosevelt a memorandum at Tehran on 30 November 1943 on the allocation of Italian ships to the Soviet Union. Prepared at Harry Hopkins' instance in case the question came up at the conference, it was cleared by Marshall, King, and Arnold, and signed by Admiral Leahy.

The original Soviet request was one battleship, one cruiser, eight destroyers, four submarines, and 40,000 tons of merchant shipping. Washington had agreed in principle to a one-third share of the Italian fleet. Moscow could not man that much now. The chiefs warn that handing ships over at once would hurt the war in Italy, might drive Italian crews to scuttle them, and would hand the enemy propaganda. They recommend keeping the one-third principle for ships transferred to other powers, but deferring any allocation of naval ships until Allied offensive operations in Italy are finished.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d495:
Closing day at the Second Cairo Conference, December 6, 1943, still produced a memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff, printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The American chiefs had spent the conference pressing their strategic case against their British counterparts. Their papers framed the joint sessions.

A memorandum written on the final day usually gathers a side's last positions before the record closes. For the American chiefs, Cairo ended weeks of argument begun at Tehran over where the next great blows would fall. Readers can use this paper to see the United States' military thinking at the exact moment the conference's conclusions were being fixed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d95: Stettinius wrote to Wallace Murray, the State Department's Adviser on Political Relations, on November 5, 1943.
