Either answer is useful: a real link would open a new research direction, while a clean separation would stop a tempting but false lead. The catalogue itself becomes a reference for any later study of melatonin and the brain.
plos-pone-0011595:
Jennifer Frost and co-authors tested gene imprinting in human placental stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Imprinted genes are used from only one parent's copy, and the largest known cluster sits around the KCNQ1 gene. In that cluster, some genes are imprinted in both mice and humans, while others differ between the two species.

The team checked three genes near the cluster ends, plus the decorin gene, in human trophoblast stem cells. None of the three showed imprinted use in these cells. The result sharpens the map of which genes carry a parent-of-origin stamp in early human development.
plos-pone-0011695:
David de Lima Morais and Paul Harrison compared RNA quality control across mammals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes can be spliced in alternative ways, changing what a protein does or where it goes. When splicing is paired with nonsense-mediated decay, the cell can also use the system to control how much of a message survives.

The authors investigated whether candidacy for this decay is conserved at genome scale. They found large-scale evidence that it is shared across mammals. A shared system suggests RNA proofreading is an ancient, deeply kept feature of mammalian biology rather than a species-by-species improvisation.
plos-pone-0011795:
Scott Houck and John Clark studied a stress protein that also serves the eye lens, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human alphaB crystallin is a small heat shock protein forming large, varied complexes. It modulates the balance between tubulin and the microtubule rods built from it, through a dynamic mechanism that was poorly understood.

The authors show that constant subunit exchange within the crystallin complex underlies that regulation of microtubule assembly. A shape-shifting helper thus tunes the cell's skeleton. The second job reveals versatility in a protein best known for keeping the lens clear.
plos-pone-0011895:
Gerald Gartlehner and co-authors published in 2010 an umbrella review, a review of reviews, on whether medicines work differently in men and women. Sex shapes disease risk, illness patterns, and life span, and scattered studies had reported sex differences in drug benefit and harm. No broad map of that evidence existed.

Gathering systematic reviews across treatments, the team assessed where efficacy and safety genuinely differ by sex and where claims rest on thin data. Their synthesis supports dosing and prescribing that treat sex as a real variable rather than a footnote. It also exposes how often trials still fail to report results separately for women and men.
plos-pone-0011995:
Barney Graham and a large team reported in 2010 a setback for an early HIV vaccine design. The vaccine mixed B and T cell targets from four subtype B HIV strains, delivered as peptides in an oily adjuvant. Healthy, low-risk adult volunteers received it to test safety and immune response.

The mixture was immunogenic, meaning it did provoke immune responses, but it also caused sterile abscesses at injection sites and unacceptable reactogenicity. A vaccine people cannot tolerate cannot be used, however good the lab numbers look. The report closes that formulation's path and warns vaccine makers that this adjuvant pairing carries a real cost in volunteers.
plos-pone-0012095:
Steen Villumsen, Rebecca Pedersen, Karen Krogfelt, and co-authors improved a lab test for leptospirosis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease spreads from animals to people, is common in much of the world, and is often missed. Its signs can look like flu at first, yet it can also move on to organ failure, so a fast and sure test matters a great deal.

Blood tests that read the germ's DNA can confirm the disease, but only if enough clean DNA can be pulled from a blood sample. The team refined that extraction step using blood cultures, making the DNA test more reliable. A better test helps doctors start the right treatment sooner, before mild illness turns severe.
plos-pone-0012195:
Benjamin Pitcher, Robert Harcourt, and Isabelle Charrier studied how fast sea lion mothers and pups learn each other's voices, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Australian sea lions raise pups in crowded colonies where a mother returning from the sea must find her own pup among hundreds. Voice recognition solves that problem, but how soon after birth it works, and which side learns first, varies between species.

Their tests show the recognition develops remarkably fast on this breeding colony. Missing the window would cost a pup its meals, so speed is survival. The work adds a case to the science of animal communication, and it helps wildlife carers judge how disturbance at colonies affects the youngest animals.
plos-pone-0012295:
Michael Zaragoza, Joseph Fass, Marta Diegoli, and co-authors hunted mitochondrial DNA variants in heart muscle diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mitochondria carry their own small genome, passed only from mother to child, and its mutations can cause inherited heart failure. A complication is mixture: a person can carry some normal and some mutated copies, and the proportions shape how sick they become.

Using next-generation sequencing, which reads DNA at great depth, the team discovered and evaluated variants in patients with cardiomyopathy. Deep reading can spot low-level mixtures older tests missed. Better variant catalogs turn a confusing genetic test into guidance a family can act on.
plos-pone-0012395:
Juan García-Arriaza, José Nájera, Carmen Gómez and co-workers profiled an HIV vaccine candidate in mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The candidate, MVA-B, uses a weakened poxvirus to carry four HIV proteins into the body. Which immune responses a vaccine must raise to block HIV is still unknown, so careful profiling of each candidate matters before human trials.

The team measured the strength and type of mouse immune responses and tested whether deleting certain virus genes made responses stronger. The deletions did boost key responses. Profiling of this kind helps vaccine designers pick the best version to carry forward, a slow but vital step toward an effective HIV vaccine.
plos-pone-0012495:
Xianfu Yi, Yu-Dong Cai, Zhisong He and colleagues predicted where DNA spools sit along the genome, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Eukaryotic DNA wraps around histone spools called nucleosomes, and their positions decide which genes are open for use. The authors tested whether the binding sites of gene switch proteins can forecast those positions.

Their predictor uses the pattern of transcription factor binding sites to place nucleosomes along a sequence. Where switches gather, spools tend to give way. A good forecast helps researchers read new genomes and understand how cells keep needed genes reachable while packing away the rest into tight chromatin.
plos-pone-0012595:
Laxman, Sutter and Tu published a yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject is the yeast metabolic cycle, a rhythm in which growing yeast cells swing between high and low oxygen use. Most work on that rhythm had tracked whole cultures at once. The team instead asked how single cells behave inside a cycling group.

To watch one cell at a time, they used glowing reporter tags tied to genes that switch on and off with the cycle. The films let them see whether each cell keeps time with its neighbours or drifts on its own. That single-cell view helps explain how a whole culture can pulse in step.
plos-pone-0012795:
Hernandez-Martinez, Navarro-Cerrillo, Caccia and co-authors studied a moth that no longer fears the main biological pesticide. Bacillus thuringiensis, or Bt, is the most used microbe for killing crop pests. The beet armyworm Spodoptera exigua has evolved resistance, threatening that tool's future.

Their 2010 study found the resistant moths keep their gut defence response against Bt switched on all the time. A defence that never sleeps may carry costs elsewhere in the insect's life. Knowing the trick helps design ways to slow or undo resistance.  Gut responses were compared between resistant and normal moths directly.
plos-pone-0331995:
Mathew Kipsum and colleagues field-tested a new mosquito net that stacks three defences against malaria in western Kenya. Standard nets rely on one insecticide family, and resistant mosquitoes are eroding their value. The 2026 evaluation put the triple net through laboratory assays, tunnel tests, and experimental huts against resistant local mosquitoes.

The net combines a pyrethroid, a growth regulator that sterilises mosquitoes, and a synergist that blocks detox enzymes. In laboratory assays it killed about nineteen of twenty mosquitoes and stopped a similar share from feeding, across repeated washes. Judged against two rival dual nets and a standard net, it met the study's comparison bars. Kipsum and colleagues add evidence for multi-ingredient nets where resistance bites.
plos-pone-0335995:
The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill harmed Gulf Coast families in many ways. Mothers lost jobs, income, and daily stability. Ariane Lisann Rung and colleagues asked whether those losses hurt children's mental health. Their study covered about four hundred forty-five mother and child pairs. All lived in Louisiana. The paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Oil exposure alone showed no direct link to child outcomes. But harder-hit mothers reported greater loss of resources. Greater loss then went with worse mental health scores in their children. The children averaged about thirteen years old. The authors draw a practical lesson. Disaster aid that restores household resources may shield children indirectly.
plos-pone-0336195:
Michael Agyemang Kwarteng, Ngozika Esther Ezinne, and co-authors surveyed optometry students across ten Nigerian universities about anxiety, depression, and stress, using a standard twenty-one-item screening scale. Their 2026 web survey drew four hundred seventy-four students, mostly in their early twenties, and linked symptom levels to background factors.

Half the students reported depressive symptoms, and about fifteen percent rated them severe or worse. Severe anxiety affected more than a third, and a quarter carried all three conditions at once. Nearly half had at least two overlapping problems. Women faced significantly higher odds of depression and of overall distress than men. The authors urge structured mental health support and prevention inside optometry training programs, arguing the burden is too large to treat as private struggle.
plos-pone-0338995:
Lanchuan Zhang and co-authors surveyed outdoor workers in Chengdu, China, about suboptimal health, the grey zone between feeling well and being ill. Drivers, construction workers, security guards, and couriers spend long days exposed to weather and strain, yet their in-between health complaints rarely reach doctors. The team used a standard sub-health scale on just over seven hundred valid responses.

Four in five workers showed some degree of sub-health, a strikingly high share. Drivers fared worst, then guards, builders, and finally couriers. Age, years spent working outdoors, marital status, family size, income, drinking, and regular exercise all connected with the condition. The authors call for measures aimed at these drivers of decline, arguing that catching workers in the grey zone is cheaper than treating full illness later.
plos-pone-0341995:
Youjin Lee and colleagues present a computer method for spotting early cognitive decline from brain scans, in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper. They used a type of PET scan that shows how the brain uses sugar, a signal that weakens as Alzheimer's disease develops. Their approach feeds the scan into the model at two scales at once: fine detail across the whole brain, and average values for set regions.

Trained on scans from a large Alzheimer's research programme, the combined model sorted people with decline from healthy peers more accurately than either scale alone. Sensitivity to real decline improved the most. Better scan reading could support earlier diagnosis, when treatment and planning help most.
plos-pone-0344395:
Victor Luckyboy Dzramado, Obed U. Lasim, and Emmanuel Oduro turn research on HIV treatment in Ghana into a set of policy proposals. Sticking with daily antiretroviral drugs keeps the virus down, yet many patients miss doses. Their 2026 article builds on a large mixed-methods study of two thousand patients in the Ashanti Region and the barriers they face.

The authors propose four structural fixes rather than more lectures to patients. Travel support would cut missed visits, community refill points would ease drug access, clinics could trim waits and protect privacy, and income plus food support would tackle poverty barriers. Each proposal is framed as a testable bet for officials working with tight budgets.
plos-pone-0344895:
Raquel V Oliveira and Elizabeth Culatta followed more than thirteen hundred young people with heavy justice-system contact, asking how different kinds of contact relate to mental health. Their 2026 PLOS One paper uses a long-running American study that tracked these youths across ten waves from 2000 to 2010.

Arrests and stays in institutions lined up with more anxiety, depression, hostility, and unusual thoughts at the same point in time. Court appearances, a milder contact, lined up with symptoms that grew later instead. Drug use and crime involvement tracked with symptoms throughout. The authors say even light contact can act as a lasting stressor for young people.
plos-pone-0345895:
Caizhen Chen and Xiuguo Zhang studied whether a common blood protein can warn of leg vein clots before hip fracture surgery. Their patients were all aged eighty or over with a break between the hip and thigh bone. The 2026 study reviewed records for close to fifteen hundred such patients admitted over eight years.

Patients with lower albumin, the protein measured, had more clots found before surgery. Each step up in albumin came with slightly lower odds of a clot, and the pattern was steady rather than curved. The link held in most patient subgroups and in checks designed to test its strength. Chen and Zhang say albumin may help flag patients who need the closest clot watch, pending further study.
plos-pone-0346095:
Yi Huang and colleagues compared the blood health of Yangtze finless porpoises living in two parts of Poyang Lake, China's largest freshwater lake. These endangered river porpoises were examined at two sites holding nineteen and six animals, with blood counts and chemistry set against known healthy ranges. Statistical methods teased apart which differences truly belonged to the habitat rather than to individual quirks.

Porpoises at the Piaotou site looked healthier overall, with stronger oxygen-carrying capacity, better nutrition markers, and livelier metabolism. The Jinxi Lake animals showed signs of clotting activation or inflammation, very low counts of one white cell type, and more values straying outside healthy ranges. The authors use the contrast to argue that conservation for this species must be habitat-specific, since one lake holds pockets of very different living conditions.
plos-pone-0346695:
Evie A Malaia and co-authors recorded brain waves from Deaf adults who sign in Austrian Sign Language while they watched videos of signing and of other human movement. The team asked how a lifetime of using a visual language, and simple ageing, reshape the brain's habit of predicting what comes next. That habit is well studied in hearing people but little explored in the visual channel.

Older and more experienced signers showed brain responses that locked more tightly onto the flow of linguistic movement, with shifts in signal complexity over the front and sides of the head. Experience, in other words, keeps refining prediction rather than letting it fade. The authors say language leaves its mark on prediction through whichever sense carries it, hearing or sight.
plos-pone-0346995:
Rasha Alkholy, Penny Bee, Rebecca Pedley, and Karina Lovell wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It reports a qualitative study carried out in the United Kingdom with older adults from varied cultural backgrounds. The topic is what these adults believe helps them cope when they feel anxious.

The study is guided by a framework from Leventhal about how people make sense of a health problem and manage their own response to it. Through participants' own accounts, the authors examine which coping strategies older adults trust and why. The findings speak to clinicians and service planners who support mental health in later life across mixed communities.
plos-pone-0347495:
Antonis Koutsoumpis and colleagues ran a cross-cultural test of a fashion myth: that horizontal stripes make the wearer look wider. In fact, laboratory vision studies find striped figures judged slimmer. Across Greece, the Netherlands, and Taiwan, the team's 2026 experiments first confirmed that people everywhere believe stripes widen, then asked them to judge dresses in a perception task.

The striped dress was again seen as thinner than a plain one of equal width. Belief and perception interacted lopsidedly: people who believed stripes slim saw the dress as slimmer still, while believers in the widening myth showed no matching distortion. The asymmetry held across all three countries, suggesting a universal quirk of vision and belief.
plos-pone-0347595:
Hideki Kawai and colleagues asked whether heart scans taken a year or more into treatment can warn of future trouble in cardiac sarcoidosis, a condition where inflammatory clusters damage the heart. Seventy-nine patients on immune-suppressing therapy had sugar-based tracer scans, which light up where heart tissue is inflamed and hungry. The team then tracked deaths, dangerous rhythms, device shocks, and heart failure admissions.

Patients whose scans still showed uptake suffered more major events over the following two years, although the signal weakened in adjusted models and over longer horizons. Among patients whose hearts still pumped strongly, event rates stayed low regardless of scan results, and repeat scans showed inflammation usually cooling on treatment. The authors see the scan as one useful clue among several, strongest when combined with pumping function.
plos-pone-0347695:
Preeclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy, can worsen fast, and few treatments slow it. Kehinde S Okunade and colleagues present a trial plan, in PLOS One in 2026, testing whether a common antioxidant drug can delay that worsening in Lagos, Nigeria.

About one hundred fifty women diagnosed early, between roughly six and eight months of pregnancy, will take a daily tablet of the drug or a look-alike placebo alongside normal care. Neither patients nor staff will know who gets which. The main measure is how many days pass before the disease advances. Results are not yet available; the trial runs through 2028.
plos-pone-0348195:
Haoge Shou and colleagues tested how adding yttrium, a rare earth metal, changes magnesium under repeated uneven loading. Light magnesium alloys suit cars and aircraft, yet they slowly stretch out of shape under cycles, a flaw called ratcheting. Pure magnesium and a magnesium yttrium alloy were cycled and then examined under electron microscopes.

Pure magnesium was stronger in a single pull, but the alloy resisted cycle drift far better. It hardened as cycles ran and lasted much longer before failing. Microscopy showed dense tangles of a hard to trigger slip type in the alloy, spreading strain evenly. Alloy designers can borrow that trick to build lighter parts that hold shape under vibration.
plos-pone-0348495:
Shinya Kato, Akihiro Yoshida, and co-authors tested a compound from licorice root against dental plaque, comparing it with a common antiseptic used in mouthwashes. The licorice compound was already known to kill plaque bacteria and slow new biofilm growth, but its effect on plaque already formed was untested. Their 2026 lab study grew plaque biofilms for a day, then applied each agent and counted living and dead bacteria.

The licorice treatment cut the number of living bacteria versus a control solvent. More unusually, it loosened the biofilm itself: the liquid above treated samples turned cloudiest, showing the most shed material, well beyond the antiseptic. The authors suggest the compound strips plaque off surfaces by a route different from simple killing, which could help prevent gum disease.
plos-pone-0348595:
Ferozkhan Jadhakhan, Deborah Falla, and Alexander Dallaway follow adults hospitalized after bone and muscle injuries to see who develops lasting post-traumatic stress symptoms. Such symptoms hamper recovery and quality of life. Their 2026 study reanalyzes a cohort of one hundred twenty-five patients at a British major trauma center, measuring symptoms just after injury and again at three and six months.

Nearly everyone crossed the symptom threshold in the raw first days, a figure the authors tie to the early timing and sensitive cut-off. By three months about a quarter still qualified, and fewer by six. Road crashes raised the risk compared with falls. Oddly, higher early anxiety and fear of movement linked with lower later risk in the models, inviting closer study of early coping.
plos-pone-0348695:
Lucas Praetzel and colleagues ran a small pilot study on a trick to make prostate cancer easier to see on scans. The scans rely on a protein called PSMA, which sits on prostate cells but is sometimes too scarce to detect. Earlier lab work suggested the drug dutasteride can raise PSMA levels. Four patients in this 2026 study took the drug for one week between two scans.

Signal strength rose in every patient after the drug course. Biopsies then confirmed cancer in the brightened spots, while one spot that faded proved cancer-free. With only four patients, the authors call the result a promising lead: a short drug course before scanning might catch tumours that would otherwise stay hidden.
plos-pone-0348895:
Haoran Zhu and colleagues present HBGCN, a neural network that predicts which drugs will act on which proteins, the first step in finding new medicines and new uses for old ones. Testing every drug against every target in a laboratory is impossible, so prediction narrows the field. Their network learns from a web of mixed biological entities, drugs, proteins, genes, and their relationships, passing messages along both direct and indirect paths.

On benchmark datasets the model performed competitively with leading methods. Case studies showed it surfacing plausible treatment candidates and highlighting the proteins and gene patterns behind its predictions. Predictions that come with a mechanism attached are far more useful to drug hunters than bare scores, because they suggest the experiments to run next.
plos-pone-0349295:
Sofia Kouki and colleagues tested whether machine-assisted image analysis can describe the grains inside archaeological mudbricks as reliably as a human expert. Mudbrick has been a building material since the first farming villages, and grain size and shape reveal how builders chose and prepared their mud. The standard expert method, counting points under a microscope, is slow and varies between analysts.

Their workflow uses a clustering algorithm on microscope images to extract grain size, sorting, and shape automatically. They applied it to forty-five images from two distant sites: Artaxata in Armenia and Los Villares in Spain. Faster, repeatable measurement would let archaeologists compare building traditions across regions without years of microscope work by specialists.
plos-pone-0349395:
Cong Hien Dinh and Anh Vu Le led a plan for a robot that cleans aircraft cabins. Planes turn around fast between flights, so cleaning must be quick. Cabins are tight and oddly shaped. Normal cleaning robots do not fit well. This robot can change its own shape. The 2026 plan splits the work into two stages.

First, the robot cleans open areas like aisles at full size. It skips the seat rows. Then it shrinks and cleans the tight spots it skipped. A search method based on evolution picks the best order of visits. It also counts the energy cost of each shape change. In tests based on real cabins, the plan beat standard methods on both time and energy.
plos-pone-0349595:
Road agencies must budget upkeep before damage forces costly rebuilds, and Chunyan Jia and colleagues forecast those preventive costs for expressways in Xinjiang, China. Their 2026 PLOS One study built a separate tuned model for each of three treatments: filling cracks, sealing surfaces, and laying new overlay.

Each model pairs a proven predictor with a nature-inspired tuning search: fruit fly, hiking, and swarm methods respectively. Tuning lifted accuracy notably in each case, with the crack-filling model explaining most cost variation. The authors argue one general model blurs real differences between treatments, and agencies should forecast each treatment on its own terms.
plos-pone-0349795:
Zac Tran and colleagues asked whether liver transplant patients who receive truly enormous amounts of fluid and blood face worse survival than those receiving merely massive amounts. Liver transplants often bleed heavily, and twenty liters or more marks an extreme group. The single-center study matched patients on recipient, donor, and operative traits so the comparison was fair.

Records from 2009 to 2023 covered adults whose total fluid around surgery reached at least ten liters. Outcomes included deaths at ninety days, at three years, and overall. Knowing whether the extreme-volume group carries extra risk beyond illness severity helps teams judge prognosis and plan intensive care. Such patients form a distinct, fragile group in transplant practice.
plos-pone-0349895:
Tomoko Matsumoto and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study tracking exclusionary nationalism in prewar Japan through newspaper language. Their marker is how readily Japanese newspapers accepted or rejected foreign loanwords, a quiet signal of openness toward outsiders. The team analyzed more than three hundred thousand articles published between 1912 and 1943 and applied a change-point method to find when attitudes shifted.

The signal of exclusionary nationalism appeared in 1936 and then swung up and down rather than climbing steadily toward the Pacific War. Attitudes distinguishing future enemies from allies were already visible in the 1920s. The authors offer the loanword approach as a quantitative way to date and size nationalist turns in other countries and periods.
plos-pone-0350095:
Ja-Ho Koo and Dimitri P Solomatine led a study of flood planning for dams. Forecast tools spawn thousands of paths a river might take. No team can plan for them all. So the set must shrink, but stay true. The team grew paths with a learning model that states its own doubt. Then they tried four ways to prune the set.

The model caught the flow's rhythm and scored well short-term. It still missed peak floods, for lack of past data. One pruning method, based on energy distance, kept the set's stats most true. Plain distance methods kept the wild flood paths best. Those paths matter most for safety. The team lays out the trade-offs for dam crews.
plos-pone-0350295:
Noelia Rodríguez-Blanco and colleagues surveyed nursing students in the province of Alicante, Spain, about adult vaccination. Their cross-sectional study, published in 2026, asked what students knew about the national adult vaccine schedule and how they felt about recommending vaccines. More than five hundred students from three universities answered the survey in spring 2025.

Nearly four in ten students did not know the adult vaccination schedule, though knowledge improved in later years of the degree. Attitudes toward vaccination were mostly positive, and many students said they would recommend vaccines to patients. The gap between goodwill and knowledge points to a clear fix in how nursing courses teach adult immunization.
plos-pone-0350395:
Can Guo, Tang Liu, and their co-authors studied whether physical weakness in older adults raises the risk of osteomyelitis, a serious bone infection. Their 2026 study used health records from the UK Biobank, a large British health database that followed hundreds of thousands of adults. They compared people who later developed the infection with similar people who did not.

Weakness was scored with five simple signs, including slow walking and a weak grip. People classed as pre-frail had clearly higher odds of bone infection, and those classed as frail had odds close to three times higher. The risk rose step by step across the groups. The results suggest that spotting frailty early could help doctors protect patients from a hard-to-treat infection.
plos-pone-0350495:
Akinori Tawaraya and Atsushi Keyaki studied older patients in hospital with aspiration pneumonia, where food or fluid slips into the lungs. Early checks of swallowing and early return to eating by mouth can aid recovery, yet timing varies. A new pathway tightened teamwork between doctors and speech therapists to make those calls faster and more alike.

Three hundred patients aged sixty five and older were compared, with and without the pathway. Patients on the pathway had close to four times the odds of eating by mouth within two days. Late swallowing checks cut those odds. Early eating showed no clear rise in harms like longer stays or repeat pneumonia in early checks.
plos-pone-0350695:
Takuya Hidaka and co-authors in Japan reported a new laboratory method in 2026 for watching a key cell signal inside single cells. The signal is phosphorylation, a small chemical tag that switches proteins on or off, and it is usually too scarce to measure one cell at a time.

Their system labels the proteins of one cell, pulls out the tagged ones with antibodies, and reads them with a custom microscope that can spot single molecules. Tested on human cells treated with a drug, it showed that cells differed widely from each other in ways that bulk tests hide. Such detail could help explain why cell signals vary so much.
plos-pone-0350895:
Yunjing Li and colleagues tested whether steady general-practice care helps older patients who live with both type two diabetes and heart or vessel disease. Two hundred patients leaving a hospital in Qinhuangdao, China, were split by chance into two groups. One got personal health teaching, community follow-up visits, and lifestyle coaching for a year; the other got routine discharge advice.

After a year, the managed group had stayed on its recommended medicines, while the routine group had let several slip. Smoking fell only in the managed group, and its members ate better and moved more. Blood sugar and cholesterol improved in both groups, but the managed patients held wider clinical gains. The trial supports ongoing primary care over one-time advice for this high-risk group.
plos-pone-0351295:
Sisi Zhuang and Lili Zuo compared blood chemistry in children with sepsis, a severe response to infection that can harm many organs. Using a public data set, they contrasted cases caused by bacteria with cases caused by viruses, and with healthy children. Their tools sorted hundreds of small molecules found in blood serum.

Fourteen molecules stood out between the groups, mostly tied to how the body handles nitrogen and a few key building blocks for proteins. Three of them, choline, glutamate, and glutamine, separated bacterial cases from viral cases especially well. Computer models built on them sorted cases with high accuracy. If later work confirms them, such markers could help doctors tell the cause sooner and choose treatment faster.
plos-pone-0351395:
Ivaneliza Simionato de Assis and colleagues surveyed more than four hundred nurses in primary care in Parana state, Brazil, about follow up care for babies born early. Early birth affects about one in ten births worldwide and drives deaths in young children. A standard tool scored five areas, from hospital discharge planning to family support, and maps showed how scores varied by place.

Discharge planning scored worst, with most ratings judged inadequate. Family support scored best, with most ratings good. Home visits, child health checks, and links between services sat in between. Nurses see family care as a strength to build on, while the handoff from hospital to clinic needs urgent repair.
plos-pone-0351495:
Rie Shimoju studied a brain relay point for touch in male rats, and how it shapes seeking a pleasant stroke. Gentle rhythmic stroking makes rats call with high happy sounds and come back for more. A calming drug was placed into the relay, which takes touch signals from the spine toward higher brain areas, to quiet it for a short time.

With the relay quieted, rats stopped approaching for the reward, yet their happy calls during stroking barely changed. Basic feeling and movement stayed intact. Seeking and feeling thus split apart in the brain: the relay seems needed to act on wanting touch, but not to voice pleasure once touch arrives.
plos-pone-0352095:
Pokushalov and colleagues, in a 2026 trial, test whether a group therapy program can lower the body's stress hormones. Long-term stress strains the system that releases cortisol, the main stress hormone, yet trials rarely measure it richly. Their program mixes social and emotional skills training, slow breathing with biofeedback, and reframing of stressful thoughts.

Sixty adults were assigned at random to the eight-week program or to an active comparison program of equal length. Stress output was measured from saliva collected across three days, and from hair, which stores a month-by-month record. The therapy group cut daily cortisol output far more than the control group, and the gain held at six months. Related measures, including a second stress chemical in saliva and hair cortisol, also fell further. The authors say the study shows talk and breathing work can leave a measurable mark on body chemistry.
plos-pone-0352395:
Pongkwan Yimsaard and seven colleagues study cannabis and sexual health among young Bangkok clinic visitors. Their 2026 mixed-method study follows Thailand's cannabis decriminalisation. Two hundred adults aged eighteen to twenty-four at sexual health clinics run by key-population groups completed surveys. Records added laboratory results for HIV and other infections. Fifteen cannabis users and fifteen non-users sat for deep interviews. The clinics serve groups at HIV risk, including gay men and transgender women.

About twenty-two percent of participants had used cannabis in the last month. Statistical tests then linked use patterns with sexual and prevention behaviours. Interview themes added the reasoning behind the numbers: how users see cannabis affecting desire, caution, and condom or medication use. Evidence of this kind was scarce for the new policy era. It gives Thai health services a grounded picture of where cannabis, sex, and HIV prevention actually intersect for young people.
plos-pone-0352995:
Eunju Jang, Ki Yoon Moon, and Sang Seob Yun ask a pointed question. Do years on dialysis before a kidney transplant shadow the years after it? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It used records from South Korea. They followed more than eighteen hundred first-time recipients. The patients were treated between 2006 and 2021. Each was sorted by how long dialysis had lasted before surgery. One group had never dialysed at all.

Patients in the longest-dialysis group died at notably higher rates. Their dialysis had averaged close to nine years. Those transplanted early fared better. The link with losing the new kidney was weaker. It was also inconsistent, especially for deceased-donor organs. The message for waiting-list policy is plain. Time on dialysis is not neutral, and earlier transplantation saves lives.
plos-pone-0353195:
Hiratsuka and colleagues built a simple branching model in a 2026 study to estimate which patients with advanced cancer live at least a year. Patients well enough to attend clinics face hard choices about care, and most older tools predict only weeks or months ahead. The team drew on a Korean group study of two hundred patients whom doctors expected to live a year or less.

Three easy-to-get measures split patients into four groups with different outlooks. The model matched real outcomes closely in repeat testing. Average survival in the group was well under a year, which underlines the stakes. After checks in other settings, such a short tool could help doctors raise care planning talks at the right time.
plos-pone-0353295:
Querino da Silva and colleagues reviewed new marker candidates for bowel inflammation diseases in a 2026 paper. Crohn's disease and related conditions are hard to diagnose and manage because standard tests can miss activity and patients respond unevenly to drugs. The review gathered work from five databases on gene, protein, and microbe markers plus imaging and sensor tools.

Candidate markers were sorted by use: early diagnosis, tracking activity, forecasting course, and predicting drug response. Artificial intelligence tools that combine many signals drew special attention. The authors frame these markers as steps toward care matched to each patient, while noting that most candidates still need strong proof in clinics before routine use.
plos-pone-0353395:
Mohammad Najeh Samara and three colleagues ask leaders at a veterans' nursing home in New York what makes recreational therapy succeed or stall, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Nineteen senior staff completed a detailed survey mixing scores with written answers. Recreational programmes — exercise, arts, group activities — are central to wellbeing for ageing veterans, yet their organisational supports are rarely examined.

Leaders rated the programme effective overall, with physical wellbeing the strongest gain, and praised the variety of activities above all. The glaring weakness was resources: a capacity index under thirty percent signalled critical strain. Engaged residents and committed staff rose together in the ratings. The authors offer their analysis as a planning tool for administrators.
plos-pone-0353695:
Shao, Gong, and Shen tested two blood ratios as warning signs in severe pneumonia in a 2026 study. Records covered nearly two hundred adults treated at one Chinese hospital over three years. Both ratios combine routine lab values tied to inflammation and nutrition, so they cost nothing extra to compute.

Patients who died had higher values of the first ratio than survivors. People below the chosen cutoffs for either ratio survived at much higher rates over their hospital stay. The first ratio predicted death more accurately than the second. Simple ratios like these could help doctors spot high-risk pneumonia patients early, when closer watch matters most.
plos-pone-0354595:
Aina Li and co-authors search in 2026 for genes that link kidney stones to vessel lining failure, a step toward hardened arteries. People with kidney stones face higher risk of vessel disease, but shared mechanisms were unclear. Three public datasets were mined for genes changed in both conditions, then a shrinking regression picked candidate markers and lab checks confirmed expression in stone samples.

Two markers stood out as key, with one clearly overactive in stone tissue. Network work tied them to cell sticking, adhesion, and recycling pathways, plus immune cell patterns. Drug prediction flagged several cancer drugs as possible matches for one marker. Personal treatment ideas remain early.
plos-pone-0354695:
Jiejun Yuan and four colleagues published this 2026 simulation study of tunnel flooding disasters in karst rock. Water flowing through limestone cavities slowly washes out the loose fill inside them, until a sudden inrush can flood a tunnel. Using a particle-based computer method, they varied fill grain size, squeezing stress, and water speed.

Their key signal was a bending point in how fast particles were being lost, which marks the turn toward collapse. Safe warning ranges differed sharply between fine and coarse fills. Yuan's thresholds could help tunnel crews set alarms before erosion crosses into catastrophe.
plos-pone-0354795:
José Rodríguez-Olivares and co-authors test in 2026 how well referral rules and tumour staining pick out Mexican bowel cancer patients who carry inherited risk variants. All such patients should be assessed, since results shape treatment and family testing. Gene panel testing served as the truth standard against which a risk calculator, two clinical rule sets, and protein staining were judged.

About a third of patients carried a harmful variant, most in the classic syndrome genes. One rule set caught almost all carriers but flagged many others, while another was highly specific. The calculator and staining both performed well. Panels testing many genes at once are recommended.
plos-pone-0354895:
Yan Zhang and three colleagues listen to women who are pregnant again after losing a baby, focusing on how they sleep, in this 2026 qualitative study from a hospital in Suzhou, China. Eighteen women in the late stage of pregnancy took part in semi-structured interviews about their nights. Their experiences have rarely been documented, despite the heavy grief and anxiety this group carries.

Three themes emerged. Sleep was often severely disrupted. Many forces fed the problem, from psychological burden and physical discomfort to unhelpful habits, thin support from family and friends, and too little guidance from healthcare providers. Women also struggled to manage the problem on their own. The authors urge providers to screen for physical discomfort and mental strain early, correct unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and build layered support for these mothers.
plos-pone-0355195:
Thaísa Bissoli and co-authors describe every twin birth in Brazil across a decade, using the national live birth registry. Twin pregnancies carry outsized risk, and Brazil's size means regional gaps matter. The analysis linked records into complete twin pairs. There were well over two hundred thousand pairs. Mothers were profiled by age, schooling, care use, and delivery mode. Newborn outcomes included low weight, early birth, and size mismatch within pairs.

Most mothers were in their late twenties or early thirties, had attended many prenatal visits, and delivered by cesarean at a strikingly high rate. Around three in five twins arrived early and underweight, with the heaviest burden in the richer south and southeast, while size mismatch within pairs stayed similar everywhere. Bissoli and colleagues call the pattern a standing challenge for Brazilian maternity care.
plos-pone-0355295:
Kedir Dendir and co-authors measure in 2026 iron shortage anaemia among pregnant women at their first antenatal visit in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Women at one health centre answered questions and gave blood for iron store and haemoglobin tests. Globally, iron shortage drives about half of anaemia cases, so local figures guide clinic advice.

Anaemia was uncommon in this group, and iron shortage anaemia rarer still, well below many wider estimates. Thin arm size, eating fewer meals, and eating a narrow range of foods linked strongly to the condition. The authors advise nutrition teaching for mothers and wider community studies to confirm the low rate.
plos-pone-0355395:
Jean Xavier leads a team of seven studying how children take another person's point of view through touch, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Mirror letters, b, d, p, and q, were traced on each child's stomach. The signal is ambiguous. It can be read from one's own perspective or from a facing person's. One hundred seven children aged six to seventeen took part, including children with autism or developmental coordination disorder, conditions where visual perspective taking is known to falter.

Left to choose, children in every group read the letters from their viewpoint, at similar rates. When a perspective was imposed, accuracy grew with age for all. The neurodivergent group scored lower in an imposed session, and response times diverged mainly for the decentered view. Touch, it seems, defaults to the self for everyone, and learning to flip that view is a developmental climb rather than a group dividing line.
plos-pone-0355495:
Ahmed M Sayed, Nada M Ezzelarab, and Nguyen Tien Huy compared how cancer and neurology drugs move through United States approval. They asked whether speed comes from stacking fast-track perks or from trial design. Their 2026 study reviewed nearly two hundred original approvals from 2015 to 2024. It scored each drug's bundle of expedited designations. It then examined the trials behind each approval.

Cancer drugs collected more expedited perks. They cleared regulatory review months faster than neurology drugs. Yet total time from development start to approval barely differed. Neurology trials were more often randomized, blinded, and late-stage. Cancer trials often used single groups. The contrast suggests review speed reflects the evidence package regulators accept, not just the perks a sponsor collects.
plos-pone-0355595:
Daiana Colledani and seven colleagues improve a screening tool for hikikomori, the severe and prolonged social withdrawal first described in Japan, in this 2026 study. Data came from a national survey of nearly nine thousand Italian teenagers who completed a fifteen-item questionnaire about withdrawal. The goal was to make the tool faster and more clinically useful without losing accuracy.

The researchers set a cutoff score that best separated at-risk teenagers and identified four distinct profiles that differed in anxiety, depression, impulsivity, and risky behavior. They then built an adaptive version that asks only the questions each person needs, cutting the length roughly in half while reproducing full scores closely. Packaged into an app that handles scoring and reporting, the short test could help schools and clinics spot withdrawn teenagers far earlier.
plos-pone-0355695:
Aqsa Rubab and colleagues produced a full breed profile of the Sipli sheep of Punjab, Pakistan, measuring bodies, wool, milk, reproduction, and growth in a flock at a government breeding center. Their 2026 study weighed and measured eighty-two adults, sampled wool across seasons, analyzed milk from fourteen ewes, and fitted four growth curve models to lamb records from two years.

Rams outmeasured ewes across the board, and male lambs stayed heavier at every age. One growth model, Brody's, described the breed's curve best. Autumn wool ran thicker and ram wool carried more coarse fiber than ewe wool. Pregnancy and lambing data completed the baseline. Such characterization is the necessary first step before any serious breeding or conservation program for a local breed.
plos-pone-0356295:
Dina Lelic and Frederic Marmel set out reference values for how everyday sounds feel to older listeners, in this 2026 study. Hearing researchers use a standard set of recorded sounds, from animal calls to tools and running water, to study emotion and hearing together. Until now, the benchmark ratings came mostly from younger adults, which limits studies of aging.

Ninety people in their middle and later years, all reporting normal hearing, rated each of the sounds online for pleasantness and intensity. Pleasant sounds tended to feel calmer, while unpleasant ones felt more arousing. Surprisingly, age, gender, and self-reported hearing habits did not predict the ratings. The published values now give researchers a fair comparison point when they study emotional responses to sound in older adults, including those with hearing problems.
plos-pone-0356395:
Kelly Carrasco and seven colleagues ran a pilot study in 2026 on a new kind of virtual classroom. Their system uses a green-screen trick to place students inside a recorded, wraparound video of a real lecture hall. The team wanted to know whether such a setup is workable for teaching and research, and how students remember, feel, and physically respond inside it.

Just over one hundred university students watched a prerecorded lecture this way and took tests before and after. Recall improved clearly right after the lecture, though overall scores stayed modest. Students felt moderately present in the virtual room and reported only mild discomfort, and feeling present did not predict better memory. The authors say short sessions like this are a feasible research tool.
plos-pone-0356495:
Oksana Artemchuk and colleagues followed 403 healthcare workers in six Georgian hospitals through three flu seasons, asking who actually takes the annual influenza vaccine they are urged to get. Their 2026 cohort study combined vaccination records with an attitudes survey and modeled which beliefs and traits separated the vaccinated from the never-vaccinated.

Nearly three in ten workers skipped vaccination in all three seasons. Disbelief in the vaccine's safety cut the odds of vaccination by almost three quarters, and doubts about effectiveness cut them deeply too. Workers in their forties were the most likely to vaccinate, and one hospital lagged dramatically. Job type and sex made no difference. The authors advise campaigns that argue safety head-on rather than repeating generic encouragement.
plos-pone-0356695:
Ayaka Uchiyama and coauthors published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE building a Japanese version of a scale that measures how work and private life blend together. Long hours are routine in Japan, and remote work has blurred the line further, so balancing two separate spheres fits daily life poorly. The team translated an existing work-life integration scale, surveyed more than seven hundred employed adults, and checked the tool's structure, reliability, and stability over time.

The original four-part structure did not fit the Japanese data. Analysis instead supported three parts: interference between work and life, strain between work and family, and ways work and family enrich each other. The scale held up against five established measures of conflict, enrichment, satisfaction, and mental health, and scores stayed fairly steady on retesting. Full-time and part-time workers differed in patterned ways, giving researchers a validated tool for studying Japanese workplaces.
plos-pone-0356895:
Yitian Liu, Zhou Zhao, and Kun Qi built a way to generate cartoon animations with strong, controllable feelings. They used generative AI tools. Two chronic weaknesses drove the work. Feelings often drift off-script, and characters feel generic. Their 2026 study layered prompts in a hierarchy. Each request was encoded along three lines: the feeling, the behavior, and the style. A language model read the request, and a video tool made the images.

Test runs held face, movement rhythm, and color mood in close agreement with the requested feeling. Different user profiles produced visibly different expression sizes, tempos, and styles. That showed the personal touch worked. The layered prompting also improved movement logic and fine gesture detail. The authors offer the scheme as a template for controllable creative AI.
plos-pone-0356995:
Yeoeun Lim and Moonwon Hwang compared three machines that measure the cornea's curve in everyday clinic conditions. They used 227 eyes of cataract surgery candidates. Their 2026 study matters because toric lens implants are chosen from exactly these measurements. Toric lenses correct astigmatism during cataract surgery. Prior device comparisons were run under tidy research conditions.

On average the devices agreed well. For individual patients they often did not. Predicted leftover astigmatism from device disagreements passed the meaningful line in nearly two thirds of patients. Among genuine toric candidates, up to a third had axis readings differing by an amount known to spoil correction. One device also nominated fewer candidates. The authors advise confirming measurements before committing a lens.
plos-pone-0357295:
Krzysztof Wilczyński led a team of eight authors linking blood molecules to thinking in older patients, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Tiny RNA molecules called microRNAs circulate in blood and regulate genes. The team ran a cross-sectional pilot study in a mixed inpatient and outpatient geriatric cohort, relating individual microRNAs to continuous measures of cognitive performance.

Wilczyński's RNA signatures could one day become simple blood tests for cognitive decline. Blood tests beat brain scans on cost and access, if the signals prove reliable. Pilot studies are small by design; their job is to find which molecules deserve larger trials. Cognitive decline is a growing burden as populations age, so even early leads toward cheap detection draw serious interest from clinicians and families alike.
plos-pone-0357395:
Moushumi Rani Dey and three colleagues published a pain study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They looked at how cold triggers pain signals in a cluster of nerve cells that serves the body, called the dorsal root ganglion. A sodium channel named Nav1.8, found in pain-sensing nerves, stood at the center of their work.

Dey's team showed that this channel helps control calcium signals inside the nerve cells when cold pain strikes. Calcium shifts are part of how a nerve cell fires and passes the pain message on. Pinning down the channel's role gives drug makers a concrete target: a drug that calms Nav1.8 might ease cold-triggered pain without dulling all feeling.
plos-pone-0357495:
Maria A. C. Wester Trejo and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE reviewing a decade of ANCA testing at a large Dutch teaching hospital. These antibody tests help diagnose autoimmune diseases that inflame blood vessels, but the standard testing order was set in specialist centers where the disease is common. In ordinary hospitals most positives may be false alarms, so the team re-examined over five thousand tested patients.

Only about one patient in twenty tested positive, and nearly two-thirds of those positives had no vasculitis at all; other autoimmune diseases, cancers, infections, or drugs explained many. Both tests ruled disease out well when negative, but starting with the antibody-specific test gave cleaner positives, and a second test sharpened accuracy. A second test is also recommended when a positive clashes with clinical doubt. The tailored strategy aims to cut false positives where the disease is rare.
plos-pone-0357595:
Sushma Swaroopa and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a fungus that lives inside the bark of a medicinal tree and may yield protective chemistry. Such fungi are rich sources of bioactive compounds. The team profiled the fungus's extract with advanced liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry, tested its ability to neutralize free radicals in a dish. They also modeled its main compound against a key antioxidant enzyme, and dosed mice before exposing them to gamma radiation.

One metabolite dominated the extract. Radical scavenging was real but moderate, clearly weaker than vitamin C in the same test. Computer modeling showed the main compound can sit against the protective enzyme superoxide dismutase, and in mice the extract more than doubled that enzyme's liver activity versus irradiated animals given nothing. This is early evidence of antioxidant potential worth purifying and testing further, not yet a proven radiation protectant.
plos-pone-0357795:
Jie Li and Xiaohong Wang published a 2026 control theory paper in PLOS ONE on keeping a special kind of neural network stable while it communicates over a cramped channel. These networks process complex-valued signals with time delays, and can only send sampled, compressed updates in bursts, resting between to save bandwidth. The authors design such an intermittent, quantized transmission scheme and prove mathematically when it still guarantees that the network settles exponentially fast.

Their two criteria, as solvable matrix inequalities, give the first explicit trade-off between transmission burst length and allowable rest fraction. A search procedure finds either limit once the other is chosen. Simulations on a small example network confirmed the scheme stabilizes the system while using far fewer transmissions. That quantitative link between rest time and switching wear, they argue, is what designers of networked controllers need.
plos-pone-0358195:
Qin Tong and Jun Liang studied glass-ceramics for nuclear waste in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Nuclear waste must stay locked away for thousands of years. One approach melts it into glass-ceramic material based on basalt. The pair used lanthanum, cerium, and neodymium as safe stand-ins for actinides, the radioactive elements in real waste.

Tong and Liang examined the material's structure and tested how fast the stand-in elements leach out in water. Slow leaching is the whole point: the waste form must hold its load even if groundwater reaches it. Results like these guide the design of waste forms long before any real actinides are used, keeping early testing safe and cheap.
plos-pone-0358595:
Niko Kargas leads a team of eight interviewing British military families who raise neurodivergent children, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Twelve parents described a support landscape split across health, education, welfare, and informal help, all inside a life of postings and deployments. The study asked how families find support, keep it, and what the effort costs them.

Support felt less like an entitlement than a prize repeatedly rewon. Each relocation broke clinical assessments, school arrangements, and diagnostic queues, and parents became the couriers of their own children's files, rebuilding trust with new professionals every move. Welfare services and informal networks genuinely helped, but access hinged on local knowledge and individual champions. The advocacy burden fell unevenly, often on mothers, and deployments reshuffled care at home. Families voiced pride and solidarity too, and resisted being praised as resilient when systems were the problem.
plos-pone-0358795:
Mohammad Mahboob Hussain Khan leads a team of eight authors in a 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting thunderstorms in Bangladesh. Storms there threaten lives, crops, and buildings, above all in the northeast. The authors build separate forecast models for three high risk weather stations, Sylhet, Sreemangal, and Mymensingh, using four decades of monthly records.

They test thirty-six approaches, from classic time series statistics to neural networks, with and without climate inputs such as cloud cover, pressure, temperature, and rain. Removing the seasonal pattern first helped a great deal, and tree based models came out best at each station. Cloud cover proved the strongest single clue. Station level forecasts like these could give farmers and local officials earlier, more useful warnings.
plos-pone-0359395:
Siavash Shirzadeh Barough and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article using laboratory rats. It studies early life stress and its later effects on the offspring. Adolescent male rat pups whose early life was stressful showed impaired glucose control, anxiety-like behavior, and oxidative stress.

Against those harms the authors test saffron extract, from the spice crocus, for a protective effect. Animal work like this explores how hardship at the very start of life programs later health, and whether a natural compound can soften that programming. The findings feed the wider search for ways to shield children exposed to early adversity.
plos-pone-0360395:
Hülya André, Derya Çetin Sarışık, and Arda Özçelik published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study of female volleyball players. The authors screen for three related risks: low energy availability, disordered eating, and how often the two occur together.

Low energy availability means an athlete takes in too little food energy for her training load, which can harm health and performance. Screening-based studies show how widespread the risk is in a squad or sport. Coaches, team doctors, and sports dietitians use such figures to decide when routine screening should become standard in women's volleyball.
pmc-13217195:
Chanvanichtrakool and colleagues report three cases of transient hypomyelination of infancy, a rare disorder of the brain's white matter. The condition, also called hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 19, stems from variants in the TMEM63A gene. Babies show early motor delay because myelin, the coating on nerve fibres, forms too slowly.

Unlike most such disorders, this one improves as the child grows. One case in the series had earlier come back negative on whole-exome sequencing, and only later review found the variant. That miss carries the lesson in the title: a negative first test should not end the search when a child's course still fits the disease.
pmc-13237995:
Tang and colleagues test a new way of planning knee replacement surgery around balance through the full bend. Standard planning follows the bone's shape, which often leaves the inner and outer sides of the joint loaded unevenly. Uneven load is a major reason implants work loose over time, so the team planned operations using gap balance in full flexion instead.

They planned surgery for eight subjects both ways and compared the results in a lab model. The gap-balanced plans produced more even load across the joint. If that evenness survives real surgery, personalised planning of this kind could help replacement knees last longer, sparing patients a second, harder operation.
pmc-13240795:
Su and colleagues at China Medical University Hospital in Taiwan built a voice system that turns spoken nursing notes into structured records. Typing notes by hand eats nursing time and invites omissions. Their pipeline pairs a fine-tuned speech recognizer with a large language model. Output follows the DART format of data, action, response, and teaching.

Fine-tuning on code-switching ward speech cut the transcription error rate from nearly forty-five percent to under seven. Generated notes scored well on structured classification, with fabricated content in only a small share. Monthly notes produced through the system roughly doubled after rollout. Three quarters of one hundred twenty nurses reported lighter workload and more complete records.
pmc-13241395:
Aytekin Kanadlı's team in Türkiye asked rheumatoid arthritis patients how digital tools fit their self-management. 25 patients at a southern teaching hospital gave long interviews. The mostly female group ran about 36 years old. Sorting the answers produced three themes and seven sub-themes.

Patients chiefly used digital tools to find facts and book visits. Everyday self-care support came second in their accounts. What they wanted most was one joined-up app linking them straight with their doctors. The authors urge builders to build around those stated hopes and to test new tools in trials.
pmc-13241495:
Huang and colleagues in Changchun photograph events a trillion times faster than ordinary cameras, in a single shot. Their method encodes time into the angular spectrum of a chirped light pulse. A multilayer photonic chip, designed by a reinforcement-learning algorithm, performs the encoding compactly. Neural networks then decode the frozen frames.

The system reached over eight hundred billion frames per second across six frames. It filmed picosecond laser damage and plasma blooming in metal films. Bulky optics and repeated measurements, standard elsewhere, disappear here. Huang offers the design for laser-matter studies needing cheap ultrafast eyes.
pmc-13241695:
AlAani and colleagues in Bahrain rebuilt a young man's bitten ear rim in a single operation. The twenty-seven-year-old lost the middle third of his left helical rim after a human bite. An initially sutured flap had necrosed, leaving a contour defect. Staged and advancement options were weighed first.

A modified flap from behind the ear, needing no skin graft, was chosen. It inset cleanly and restored the rim's curve. Follow-up showed stable healing, preserved ear shape, and a highly satisfied patient. The authors commend the single-stage route for similar traumatic defects.
pmc-13242395:
Reuter's team in Bochum put a VR headset on 471 people to catch a subtle eye-movement lesion. Healthy controls wore it too. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia slows the inward eye during side gaze. The group held 243 MS patients and healthy controls. Blinded software compared inward and outward movement speeds.

Agreement with bedside exams was only moderate. In MS, the headset flagged 23 cases clinicians missed; doctors caught three it missed. VR-positive patients had longer disease and worse brainstem scores. The authors propose VR eye tracking as an added digital marker needing more checks.
pmc-13242495:
Jia Song, Julie Ratcliffe, and Rachel Milte searched for a score that marks good quality of life on Australia's aged care questionnaire. Their study appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. The QOL-ACC measure became a mandatory national indicator in 2023, but staff lacked a reference point for reading its scores. The team collected self-reports from residents and proxy reports from family carers across long-term care facilities.

The analysis covered 316 care recipients, most of them women, with an average age of eighty-four. The team compared questionnaire totals against residents' own global ratings. A score of eighteen or more out of twenty-four best separated those reporting good health and good quality of life from the rest. The cut-off gives facilities a practical yardstick for routine monitoring. It can also flag where care planning and quality work should focus first.
pmc-13243195:
Emilio Peniche-Luna and colleagues report a case of pseudoxanthoma elasticum that arose without any family history of the disease. Their case report, with a short literature review, appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. A forty-four-year-old woman presented with yellowish bumps, three to ten millimeters wide, merging into cobblestone-like plaques. Eye examination had already found angioid streaks in her retina, while her heart and vessels showed no involvement.

Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is a rare disorder in which elastic tissue slowly mineralizes in skin, eyes, and arteries. Skin changes usually come first, so recognizing them can speed diagnosis and head off complications elsewhere. Because the disease touches many systems, the team sent her for a baseline cardiology check despite her lack of symptoms. The authors close by noting that new work on the molecular pathways may one day yield treatments that change the disease's course.
pmc-13243795:
Stephen Hardies and colleagues report on a newly found virus in this 2026 study from South Korea. The virus, named LSH1, infects bacteria of the genus Alishewanella and was collected, with its host, from the thin top layer of a brackish tidal reservoir.

Gene reading showed LSH1 is only distantly related to other cultured bacteria-infecting viruses, and seems to be the first member of a large, unsampled branch of the virus family tree. Microscope images revealed an unusual tail end. Protein-shape modelling then showed its tail hub is a stripped-down version of a classic design, missing the parts some viruses use to sense their host.
pmc-13246095:
Ravikulan, Falvey, and Kubovy report a serious drug reaction in this 2026 ACG Case Reports Journal article. A fifty-year-old woman whose ulcerative colitis had been limited and well controlled started atogepant, a newer migraine-prevention drug that blocks the CGRP receptor. Soon afterward she developed abdominal pain and diarrhea, and scans and scope examinations showed severe inflammation across her whole colon.

Steroids given by vein failed to settle the flare. She recovered only after the migraine drug was stopped and she received infliximab, an immune-suppressing infusion, and she remained well three months later. The authors warn clinicians to use this drug class carefully in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
pmc-13246995:
Deng, Wei, Pang, and co-authors built a database of the proteins the immune system wrongly attacks in autoimmune disease, in this 2026 Advanced Biotechnology paper. Such target proteins, called autoantigens, are the key to precise diagnosis and treatment, yet research has concentrated on a familiar few. Their resource, SPAID, covers fourteen autoimmune diseases and deliberately reaches beyond the classics.

The database works on two levels. One tier holds proteins with experimentally confirmed evidence from T-cell and antigen-presentation assays. A second, larger tier gathers candidates found by mass spectrometry in human samples, annotated with expression patterns, predicted immunogenicity, and function to guide follow-up experiments. The authors offer SPAID as a foundation for discovering new diagnostic markers and antigen-focused therapies.
pmc-13247395:
Manley, Moran, Ham, and co-authors followed teenagers whose kneecaps kept slipping out of place, in this 2026 Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine case series. Rebuilding the medial patellofemoral ligament, the strap holding the kneecap in its groove, is the standard fix, but in growing patients the growth plates are still open and surgery must respect them. The team reviewed fifty-four knees in fifty-one patients treated at one academic center between 2010 and 2019.

At an average of about eight years after surgery, only four knees had suffered further partial slips, and none had a full dislocation. No growth disturbances were confirmed, knee function scores were strong, and many patients returned to sport. The authors call the anatomic reconstruction, paired with other procedures when needed, safe and durable for adolescents.
pmc-13247795:
Connon, Park, and Turner hunted for what separates resilient adults from struggling ones after hard childhoods, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine study. Earlier work had sorted people into higher and lower mental well-being trajectories over twelve years. The team compared those groups separately among people with no adverse childhood experiences and among nearly nine hundred who had them, testing genetic, social, health, and personality predictors.

In both groups, higher well-being came with more education, better self-rated physical health, stronger social engagement and work performance, and a personality pattern of lower neuroticism and higher extraversion. Genetic well-being scores added discrimination only without adversity. The authors stress that the resilience factors they found are largely modifiable, naming concrete targets, social connection, health, and work support, for interventions after childhood adversity.
pmc-13248895: Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine retracted this 2014 rat study in 2026, and this notice records the withdrawal plainly. The paper had claimed that sodium hydrosulfide eased nerve pain in rats with a chronic constriction injury. Concerns about its figures were first raised on the post-publication site PubPeer, and further investigation by the publisher, John Wiley and Sons, found more problems. The journal therefore withdrew the article, and its results should no longer be cited as reliable evidence.
pmc-13249095:
Gupta and co-authors recount two treatment complications colliding in one patient, in a 2026 case report. A fifty-seven-year-old man with Crohn's disease taking infliximab, an immune-suppressing infusion, developed skin abscesses and spreading inflammation. Cultures grew Mycobacterium mucogenicum, a fast-growing relative of tuberculosis that rarely infects skin and favors patients with weakened immunity.

An antibiotic given first, levofloxacin, was followed within four days by a torn Achilles tendon, a known risk of that drug family. Doctors switched to two other antibiotics for six months while continuing his Crohn's therapy, and the lesions healed steadily. The authors urge early microbe hunting in such patients and caution with that antibiotic class.
pmc-13250195:
Naing and a large team report the first human trial of alomfilimab, an antibody drug aimed at a marker on immune-suppressing cells inside tumors. Their 2026 Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer paper covers patients with advanced solid tumors who had no standard options left. The drug was given alone, or with a second antibody called atezolizumab, every three weeks.

Thirty-eight patients received the drug alone, and just over one hundred received the pair. Side effects were common but judged manageable, and no patient on the single drug had a clear tumor response. Seven patients on the combination did respond, though average time without growth stayed near two months. Blood and tumor tests showed the target cells fell, so the drug hit its mark despite limited benefit.
pmc-13250695:
Evodius Rutta studies tomato losses after harvest in southern Tanzania in this 2026 paper. Climate change is often blamed for poor crops in the field, but this work looks at what happens after picking, where small farmers can lose much of their income.

Interviews and group talks with 52 farmers in the Kilolo district pointed to surprise rains, weak storage, transport delays, and slow pick-ups as the main loss drivers. Some farmers lost up to 40 percent of their crop for lack of storage. Pest losses before harvest mattered less by comparison. Rutta calls for cheap cold storage, processing options, and better training for growers.
pmc-13251095:
Tao and co-authors are the authors of the study protocol that this 2026 Retraction Note in Trials withdraws. The retracted protocol, first published in 2024, planned a randomized trial of two blood pressure drugs and clotting responses in cesarean patients under spinal anesthesia. The journal's editor-in-chief retracted it after a post-publication review.

The review found the paper's sample size, primary outcome, and secondary outcomes did not match the registered trial record. Changes to the registered trial also lacked clear explanation and any mapping to the published version. The note records that the authors disagree with the retraction, stated through author Wenhui Tao. Readers should treat the protocol as withdrawn and not rely on it.
pmc-13253895:
Khizzra Aslam and co-authors build a green light filter in a 2026 optics study. Their device uses guided-mode resonance gratings, fine ridged surfaces that trap certain light waves. A titanium dioxide coating on a one-dimensional grating lets it filter green light based on polarization, the direction light waves vibrate.

The team made the gratings with holographic lithography, giving a sloped ridge shape, and coated them by magnetron sputtering on glass-like bases. Tests showed strong polarization filtering for green light at straight-on angles. Nanoimprinting, a stamp-like copying method, could make the filters cheaply in bulk for imaging and communications use.
pmc-13255195:
Hyunjin Oh, Jihoon Kim, and Jaewoo Bai test a bacterial product against tooth decay germs in a 2026 study. Streptococcus mutans builds the biofilm that drives dental caries. The team made a neutralized postbiotic mediator from a Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strain taken from jeotgal, a fermented seafood.

The product damaged germ membranes, causing about 87 percent damage at the top dose tested. It cut biofilm formation by 83 percent at that dose and lowered output of the glue-like coating germs use to stick. Key biofilm genes were turned down, and human gut cells showed no toxicity in tests.
pmc-13256095:
Ma and colleagues built a prediction model for pneumonia after hip fracture surgery in older patients, drawing on more than two thousand cases aged sixty-five and over. Their model combined a five-item frailty index and a geriatric nutritional risk index with comorbidities and blood tests. Performance was checked by discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis, and machine learning models were compared.

The extended model discriminated well and calibrated cleanly. Lung disease, intensive care admission, low blood oxygen, poor nutrition scores, greater frailty, and a heart failure marker independently raised pneumonia risk. Random forest and gradient boosting ranked nutrition and frailty highest too, though their calibration was weaker. The authors offer the model for preoperative triage.
pmc-13260195:
Patricia Jaramillo-Álvarez and co-authors present a 2026 study of IGOR, a framework for ranking mining policies in Colombia. IGOR stands for Importance, Governance, and Robustness, and it is meant for decisions with trade-offs across social, environmental, economic, and governance concerns under deep uncertainty. It combines four tools: an importance-governance matrix, a ranking process for weighting tests, tornado sensitivity analysis, and Monte Carlo simulation, which tests many random cases by computer.

The team applied IGOR to Colombia's National Mining Development Plan 2024–2025, rating over one hundred actions. The tests were built with national partners to keep them relevant. The method produced clear scores that picked out actions that were high-impact, feasible, and resilient. Checks showed the outcomes held up under varying user preferences. The authors offer IGOR as a strict, flexible tool for other complex policy fields.
pmc-13261295:
Pedro Pau reports a 2026 case of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis presenting as fever of unknown origin in a young child. ADEM is an inflammatory disorder that strips insulation from nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. It usually causes several neurological deficits at once. A relapsing form is called multiphasic disseminated encephalomyelitis.

The patient was a previously well 4-year-old boy with prolonged fever and body-wide inflammation but no early neurological signs. Brain MRI showed multifocal demyelination, and MOG antibodies were positive. He was diagnosed with ADEM and treated with steroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He relapsed twice, which fit the multiphasic form. The case shows that ADEM can begin as an unexplained fever alone. Early imaging and antibody testing can reveal the cause.
pmc-13263295:
Miguel A García-Pérez and Rocío Alcalá-Quintana ask how best to model people's judgment of time intervals in a 2026 journal article. In duration tasks, researchers fit curves showing how often a test interval is judged longer than a standard. Other senses use the logarithm of stimulus size as the curve's input, following classic perception laws, but time studies usually use raw duration.

Simulations first showed which study designs can separate the two curve types. An experiment then ran 1,200 adaptive trials per dataset across 45 datasets. Log-duration curves fit better in most cases. Checking more than 17,000 published curves from 69 papers pointed the same way. The authors conclude duration data are generally better described against log duration.
pmc-13264995:
Somayeh Hajiahmadi and colleagues present a 2026 study of CT angiography measures for right heart failure in pulmonary hypertension, high pressure in the lung arteries. The right side of the heart fails as pressure rises, and catheter tests are invasive. The team asked whether measures from a widely available CT scan can stand in, using ultrasound as the reference.

They studied 39 adults with newly diagnosed disease not caused by left heart problems. Right heart dysfunction was present in 71.8 percent and severe pressure in 51.3 percent.
